The vacancy after Clement IV's death (Viterbo, Nov 1268) lasted from 1 Dec 1268 to 1 Sep 1271, the longest papal election; the cardinals were divided between pro-Angevin (Charles of Anjou) and anti-French factions; custom placed the election where the pope died.
facts.uncertainty: Factions hard to reconstruct exactly (Annales Piacentines vs Sternfeld)

facts.text: Viterbo's magistrates (podestà and captain) locked the cardinals in the Palace of the Popes, reduced them to bread and water, and removed the roof; some sources credit Charles of Anjou as instigator.
facts.source_location: 'ordered... the cardinals sequestered in the Palace of the Popes'; 'Other sources say it was Charles of Anjou who orchestrated...'
facts.uncertainty: Exact timing (late 1269/1270) and who ordered the roof removal disputed; makeshift roof possibly restored

facts.text: On 8 June 1270 the cardinals wrote from the 'Palatio discooperto' (uncovered palace).
Onofrio Panvinio (16th c.) attributes to Cardinal John of Toledo the quip that the room must be uncovered or the Holy Spirit would never reach them.
facts.source_location: 'According to the account of Onofrio Panvinio...'

facts.text: Three cardinals died during the vacancy and one left through illness.

facts.text: On 1 Sep 1271 the cardinals delegated to a committee of six, which chose Teobaldo Visconti (not a cardinal), then in Acre as legate with Edward's crusade; he reached Viterbo 12 Feb 1272 and was crowned in Rome 27 Mar 1272 as Gregory X.

Gregory X's Ubi periculum (7 Jul 1274, Second Council of Lyon): election after 10 days, cardinals enclosed in common without walls, guarded, food by window; after 3 days one dish, after 8 days bread, wine and water.
'Conclave' derives from Latin cum clave, 'with a key'.

facts.text: First election under the rules (Jan 1276) took one day; Adrian V suspended them, John XXI revoked them (Sep 1276); following elections lasted 7, 6, 11 and 27 months (1292–94).

facts.source_location: 'sent the cardinals a letter warning them that divine vengeance would fall upon them'; resignation

facts.text: The lantern was designed by Brunelleschi but finished after his death; Verrocchio's gilded ball was placed in 1471.
facts.source_location: Dome page: lantern; ball 1471; current ball early-1600s replacement

facts.text: Brunelleschi died in 1446 and was buried in the cathedral; his tomb was found in 1972.
It is still the largest masonry dome in the world (claim by the Opera).
facts.source_location: 'still the largest masonry vault in the world'
facts.uncertainty: Superlative depends on definition; the Pantheon (concrete) spans ~43.3 m (Treccani)

facts.text: An imagined dome already appears in Andrea di Bonaiuto's Spanish Chapel fresco (1365–67), before anyone knew how to build it.
facts.uncertainty: Fresco shows an idealised design, not Neri's model

facts.text: The drum (tambour) was completed c.1410-13; the dome springs about 54 m (Moore: 175 ft) above the cathedral floor.
facts.source_location: sgira: drum completed by 1410-13; Moore 1905 ch.2: 'springing level is a hundred and seventy-five feet above the pavement'
facts.uncertainty: Exact completion year of drum varies by source (1410-1413); height figures vary 52-55 m

facts.text: The 1420 programme says the outer shell protects the inner from damp and makes it more magnificent; build without centring to 30 braccia, then decide, 'because in building, practice teaches what is to be followed'.
facts.source_location: Moore 1905 ch.2 quoting Guasti 1857 pp.28-30: '...perchè nel murare la pratica insegna quello che si ha da seguire'
facts.corroboration: Guasti, La cupola di Santa Maria del Fiore (1857), pp.28-30 (PD)
facts.uncertainty: Translation ours; programme text is commonly attributed to Brunelleschi (with the other supervisors)

facts.text: Santa Reparata, the old cathedral, was small and in poor repair; Florence sought a cathedral to outdo rivals Pisa and Siena; the new building rose around the old church.
First stone laid in September 1296 (Opera: 8 Sept; Wikipedia: 9 Sept). Arnolfo died in the early 1300s (1302 or 1310 disputed) and work slowed.
facts.uncertainty: Exact day and Arnolfo's death year disputed

facts.text: 'Santa Maria del Fiore' alludes to Florence's name (Florentia).
In 1331 the Arte della Lana took over patronage of the cathedral works.
Giotto appointed 1334 for the campanile; died 1337 with only the first level begun; Andrea Pisano (relief panels) then Talenti completed it c.1359; 84.7 m; terrace rather than spire.
The Black Death halted work in 1348; Talenti resumed in 1349.
Francesco Talenti and successors enlarged Arnolfo's plan, including a larger octagonal crossing.
facts.source_location: Opera: current building follows Talenti's expansion

facts.text: The 1367 model rejected external flying buttresses, then standard in French Gothic.
Santa Reparata was pulled down by 1375 and the nave was finished by about 1380.

1401 Calimala competition for Baptistery doors: Sacrifice of Isaac trial panels in quatrefoil; seven semifinalists incl. Brunelleschi and Ghiberti; both panels survive in the Bargello; Ghiberti's cast largely in one piece; north doors installed 1424; east doors 1425–52; Michelangelo called them Gates of Paradise (per Vasari).
Manetti credits Brunelleschi with perspective demonstrations (Baptistery panel and mirror, c.1415–20); Alberti's Della pittura (1436) dedicated to Brunelleschi.
Brunelleschi made a brick-and-timber model with Donatello and Nanni di Banco.
Vasari's story that Brunelleschi feigned illness to expose Ghiberti is an anecdote.
Dome: two shells joined by 24 meridian and 10 parallel ribs; 463 steps to the top; 90 m floor to lantern base.
Brunelleschi designed rotating cranes, trolleys, winches; machines later studied by Francesco di Giorgio, Giuliano da Sangallo, Verrocchio and Leonardo.

About 60 masters; parapets on suspended scaffolding; food and drink sent up (Vasari's taverns a legend); 8 serious injuries; Nencio di Chello died falling from the drum in 1422; funeral, sick pay and treatment paid; work aloft voluntary with higher pay.
23 Apr 1426: wine on the cupola to be diluted by one third; 5 Jun 1426: undiluted wine allowed at the master's discretion, drunk workers dismissed.
9 Sep 1427: danger pay for stonecutters working on the cupola.
Florence fought costly wars (Milan, Lucca) and suffered recurrent plague in the 1420s–30s; Cosimo de' Medici exiled 1433, returned 1434.
Eugenius IV fled Rome on 4 June 1434, rowed down the Tiber disguised as a monk, to Florence.
Dufay's motet Nuper rosarum flores was composed for the 1436 consecration.
Laetentur caeli, the decree of union of Latin and Greek churches, proclaimed 6 July 1439 in Florence Cathedral in Latin and Greek; the union was soon repudiated.
facts.source_location: BML record: proclaimed in Santa Maria (del Fiore)

facts.text: 1436 lantern competition won by Brunelleschi over Ghiberti and others; lantern begun months before his death (April 1446); completed by Michelozzo c.1461.

Verrocchio's gilded copper ball (~2.5 m) hoisted 27 May 1471 (Landucci's diary), cross 30 May; young Leonardo in Verrocchio's workshop took part; Leonardo's later note (Ms G) on the soldering of the palla.
facts.uncertainty: Wikipedia gives 1469 for the ball; Opera's 1471 used

facts.text: Lightning struck the lantern 5 Apr 1492; on the night of 26–27 Jan 1601 the ball fell; a slightly larger ball placed 1602; marble disc marks the spot.
facts.uncertainty: Wikipedia dates the fall to 1600; Opera used

facts.text: The Pazzi conspirators attacked Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici in the cathedral during Mass, 26 April 1478; Giuliano was killed.
Vasari and Federico Zuccari painted the Last Judgement inside the dome, 1572–79.

Arnolfo's unfinished facade dismantled 1587; bare front (painted for festivals) until 19th c.; 22 Apr 1860 Victor Emmanuel II laid a first stone; competitions and a vote on the crown; De Fabris won, died 1883; Luigi Del Moro completed; inaugurated 12 May 1887, three centuries after demolition.
facts.uncertainty: Painted temporary facades for festivals per Wikipedia

facts.text: The Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore (Opera del Duomo), founded 1296, still manages the cathedral complex.
A statue of Brunelleschi in the piazza looks up at the dome.
The Papal States were territories of central Italy under papal sovereignty from 756 to 1870, covering modern Lazio, Umbria, Marche and part of Emilia-Romagna.
facts.source_location: Opening paragraph: 'territories of central Italy over which the pope had sovereignty from 756 to 1870'.
facts.uncertainty: Extent and degree of control varied over centuries (Britannica says so). Britannica's Vatican City article dates the Donation of Pippin to 754, its Papal States article to 756 (754 = promise at Quierzy/Ponthion; 756 = territories handed over).

facts.text: Pope Stephen II appealed to the Frankish ruler Pippin III against the Lombards; the Donation of Pippin provided the basis for the papal claim to temporal power.
facts.source_location: 'Early history' section: 'This Donation of Pippin (756) provided the basis for the papal claim to temporal power.'
facts.uncertainty: Date 754 vs 756 (see C01). Britannica also notes the Donation of Constantine forgery was 'probably' made around this time - do not overstate.

facts.text: Papal rule was interrupted in the Napoleonic period (France annexed Avignon in 1791 and seized other papal territory) and the popes' temporal power was repeatedly contested.
facts.source_location: Top Questions: 'France annexing Avignon in 1791 and seizing other papal territories.'
facts.uncertainty: Further interruptions (Roman Republics of 1798-99 and 1849) are well known but not yet sourced in this file - source before use.

facts.text: After 1859 most papal territories joined the Kingdom of Sardinia; by 1861 all former papal lands except Rome (and Lazio) were part of the new Kingdom of Italy; French troops protected Rome until 1870.
facts.source_location: Top Questions 'How and why did the Papal States come to an end?'
facts.uncertainty: Britannica's AI-generated 'Top Questions' summaries carry an AI warning; corroborated by Encyclopedia.com (Roman Question: Napoleon III as Pius IX's sole protector). Rome was not the only remnant: Latium around it also remained papal until 1870.

facts.text: The Italian Chamber of Deputies proclaimed Rome capital of the new kingdom on 27 March 1861, while it was still papal territory.
facts.corroboration: | STAGE C: Camera dei deputati historical portal, VIII Legislatura chronology, 27 Mar 1861: 'La Camera approva l'ordine del giorno Bon Compagni, che riafferma l'esigenza che Roma sia «ricongiunta» all'Italia' (https://storia.camera.it/cronologia/leg-regno-VIII/elenco). Senato library essay on Cavour's March 1861 speeches: Cavour says the motions all agree 'che si acclami Roma come capitale d'Italia' and backs the Bon Compagni motion (http://www.senato.it/relazioni-con-i-cittadini/biblioteca/pubblicazioni-testi/minervaweb/i-discorsi-di-cavour-alla). Treccani Atlante: Cavour 'indotto il Parlamento a dichiarare Roma capitale d'Italia, anche se come atto meramente simbolico' (https://www.treccani.it/magazine/atlante/cultura/20_settembre_1870_arrivano_i_bersaglieri_a_segnare_la_fine_del_Papa_Re.html).
facts.uncertainty: Strictly, the 27 Mar 1861 vote was a Chamber motion (ordine del giorno Bon Compagni) acclaiming Rome as capital and calling for it to be reunited with Italy. It was symbolic, not a law, and Cavour said the actual transfer would need a later vote of Parliament. 'Almost unanimous' per italiadecide.it introductory essay only.

facts.text: France's defeat at Sedan (1 Sept 1870) left Pius IX without international protection, allowing Italy to occupy Rome on 20 September 1870.
facts.source_location: 'Origins': 'after France's defeat at Sedan (Sept. 1, 1870), the pope lacked all international help ... occupying the Eternal City (Sept. 20, 1870).'
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/place/Papal-States | STAGE C: Treccani Atlante: the Franco-Prussian war and Napoleon III's fall after Sedan (1-2 Sept 1870) 'privavano Pio IX del suo alleato più importante' (https://www.treccani.it/magazine/atlante/cultura/20_settembre_1870_arrivano_i_bersaglieri_a_segnare_la_fine_del_Papa_Re.html). Esercito Italiano: after news of Sedan and the Paris republic, the government considered the September Convention lapsed (https://www.esercito.difesa.it/organizzazione/armi-e-corpi/Fanteria/Le-Specialita/I-Bersaglieri/Breccia-di-Porta-Pia).
facts.uncertainty: French garrison had already been withdrawn in summer 1870 for the Franco-Prussian War; Sedan removed any prospect of return.

facts.text: On 20 September 1870 Italian artillery opened a breach in the Aurelian Walls near Porta Pia and troops entered Rome; the papal commander signed a capitulation the same day.
facts.source_location: Treccani Dizionario di Storia (2011), 'Porta Pia, breccia di': on 20 Sept 1870 the stretch of Aurelian Walls between Porta Pia and Porta Salaria was the target of the main attack by Italian troops under Gen. R. Cadorna. After the first shots the Pope ordered papal commander H. Kanzler to limit the defence to the time needed to register the Holy See's protest; Kanzler delayed. The papal troops at Porta Pia surrendered only after an assault, as units nearest 'l'ampia breccia' (35th Bersaglieri battalion, 39th and 40th infantry) began the entry into Rome.
facts.corroboration: Treccani Atlante (2017): first two cannon shots at 5.15 a.m.; fire concentrated between Porta San Giovanni and Porta Pia; white flag shown at Porta Pia at 10.10; Bersaglieri entered; surrender signed at Villa Albani excluding the Leonine City/Vatican hill (https://www.treccani.it/magazine/atlante/cultura/20_settembre_1870_arrivano_i_bersaglieri_a_segnare_la_fine_del_Papa_Re.html). Esercito Italiano official page: order to attack the breach given at 9 a.m.; Kanzler had fewer than 16,000 men (https://www.esercito.difesa.it/organizzazione/armi-e-corpi/Fanteria/Le-Specialita/I-Bersaglieri/Breccia-di-Porta-Pia). la Repubblica (2020) narrative based on Ugo Pesci: breach open from about 9, Pius ordered capitulation about 9.30.
facts.uncertainty: Numbers differ: papal force 13,000 (Treccani Atlante) vs <16,000 (Esercito); Cadorna 50,000 (Treccani Atlante). Times differ by source (first shot 5.00-5.15; white flag ~10). Accusations over firing after the white flag are disputed (la Repubblica). Casualty numbers not sourced: do not narrate. Exact breach coordinate not sourced.

facts.text: After a plebiscite in October 1870, Rome became the capital of Italy.
facts.source_location: Treccani Atlante: 'Il referendum del 2 ottobre 1870 sancì l'annessione al Regno d'Italia della città, che, subito dopo, venne proclamata capitale.'
facts.uncertainty: Formal transfer of the capital by law in 1871 (not yet sourced precisely); narrate loosely.

facts.text: Italy's Law of Guarantees (13 May 1871) unilaterally granted the Pope honours, inviolability and an annual allowance, but no sovereign territory under international law.
facts.source_location: 'Contents' and 'Papal Attitude' paragraphs: unilateral domestic law, 'subject to revocation or suspension at any time'.
facts.corroboration: https://academic.oup.com/book/26645/chapter/195382782 (Chadwick, OUP abstract); Lateran Treaty Art. 26 abrogates 'the law dated May 13, 1871 (No. 214)'
facts.uncertainty: Whether the Vatican palaces were granted as property or only 'use' is a nuance - check full text before narrating details.

facts.text: Pius IX rejected the Law of Guarantees (encyclical Ubi nos, 15 May 1871), refused the financial grant and remained inside the Vatican as a self-described 'prisoner'; his successors to Pius XI kept this stance.
facts.uncertainty: 'Prisoner' was a protest posture, not physical captivity; popes did not appear publicly in Italian Rome, but the phrase should be framed as theirs.

facts.text: The Lateran Pacts were signed on 11 February 1929 by Cardinal Pietro Gasparri for the Holy See and Benito Mussolini for the Kingdom of Italy.
facts.source_location: Final signatures of Treaty and Financial Convention: 'PIETRO Cardinale GASPARRI  BENITO MUSSOLINI'; Treaty Art. 27 'Dated in Rome this 11th day of February, 1929'.
facts.uncertainty: Britannica's quick facts list Borgongini-Duca and Boselli as 'key people'; negotiators included Francesco Pacelli (not yet sourced). Signing location (Lateran Palace) not yet sourced.

facts.text: The Pacts comprised three instruments: a Treaty (with Annex I map), a Concordat, and a Financial Convention (Annex 4 of the Treaty).
facts.source_location: Document header: 'TRATTATO ... CONVENZIONE FINANZIARIA ... CONCORDATO'; Treaty Art. 25 references the Convention as Annex 4.
facts.uncertainty: Britannica's Lateran Treaty article mixes Treaty and Concordat articles (its 'Article 34/36' are Concordat articles).

facts.text: Treaty Art. 3: Italy recognises the Holy See's full ownership, exclusive dominion and sovereign jurisdiction over the Vatican, 'thus creating the Vatican City'; boundaries are fixed by the Annex I map.
facts.uncertainty: English versions are unofficial translations; the authoritative text is Italian (vatican.va).

facts.text: St Peter's Square is part of Vatican City but normally open to the public and supervised by Italian police up to the foot of the basilica steps.
facts.uncertainty: vaticanstate.va says boundary is a travertine/marble strip joining the outer ends of the colonnade.

facts.text: Treaty Art. 26: the Holy See declared the Roman Question 'definitely and irrevocably settled', recognised the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as capital; Italy recognised the State of the Vatican City under the sovereignty of the Supreme Pontiff; the 1871 law was abrogated.
facts.source_location: Article 26 (transcription on this page has a garbled Art. 25/26 join - cross-check with Italian text).
facts.uncertainty: Transcription error on cuni.cz page noted.

facts.text: Treaty Art. 24: the Holy See will take no part in temporal rivalries between states; Vatican City is to be considered 'neutral and inviolable territory'.

Arts. 13-16 give the Holy See ownership of the basilicas of St John Lateran, Santa Maria Maggiore and St Paul, and of the papal palace at Castel Gandolfo; listed buildings get diplomatic-style immunity and tax exemption while remaining Italian territory.
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/place/Vatican-City | STAGE C: Italian text Art. 15: buildings 'benché facenti parte del territorio dello Stato italiano, godranno delle immunità riconosciute dal diritto internazionale alle sedi degli agenti diplomatici di Stati esteri'. Art. 15 names: Dataria, Cancelleria, Propaganda Fide (Piazza di Spagna), Sant'Offizio, Convertendi, Vicariato.
facts.uncertainty: Britannica: 'extraterritorial privileges ... more than 10 other buildings in Rome and to Castel Gandolfo'. The term 'extraterritorial' is a common shorthand; the Treaty speaks of immunity. Avoid a precise count.

facts.text: Financial Convention Art. 1: Italy paid 750,000,000 lire in cash plus 5% Italian government bonds of nominal value 1,000,000,000 lire, accepted as the final settlement of the events of 1870.
facts.uncertainty: Modern-value conversions are unreliable and contested - do not give a present-day equivalent unless an economic-history source is cited.

facts.text: Concordat 1929: Catholic marriage given civil effect; religious instruction in state schools.
facts.source_location: Paragraphs on 'article 34' and 'article 36 of the concordat'.
facts.corroboration: https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/secretariat_state/archivio/documents/rc_seg-st_19290211_patti-lateranensi_it.html | STAGE C: verified in official Italian Concordat text (research/patti_it.txt): Art. 34 gives civil effect to the sacrament of marriage governed by canon law; Art. 36 extends religious instruction in public schools.
facts.uncertainty: Britannica wrongly frames these as Treaty articles in places; check against Italian Concordat text.

facts.text: Treaty Art. 1 reaffirmed Catholicism as the 'only State religion' of Italy; the 1984 Agreement (Additional Protocol) declared this principle no longer in force.
facts.source_location: Treaty Art. 1; Accordo 1984, Protocollo addizionale 'In relazione all'Art. 1'.

facts.text: The Concordat was revised by an Agreement signed on 18 February 1984 by Cardinal Agostino Casaroli and Bettino Craxi; vatican.va lists it under 3 June 1985 (exchange of ratifications); Britannica calls it 'the concordat of 1985'.
facts.source_location: Signatures 'AGOSTINO CARD. CASAROLI / B. CRAXI'; later documents cite 'l'Accordo ... del 18 febbraio 1984'.

facts.text: Britannica says the Lateran Treaty was confirmed by the Italian constitution of 1948.
facts.uncertainty: Britannica gives treaty 'effective June 7, 1929, to June 3, 1985' - misleading: 1985 date relates to the Concordat revision; the Treaty and Vatican City remain in force. Do NOT repeat Britannica's end date.

facts.text: Vatican City covers 0.44 km² (44 hectares).
facts.source_location: 'The State's territory, which covers a surface area of 0.44 km2 (44 hectares)'.
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/place/Vatican-City (Total Area 0.44 sq km / 0.17 sq mi; 'minute territory of 44 hectares (109 acres)' in Lateran Treaty article)
facts.uncertainty: vaticanstate.va History page contains a typo ('0.44 hectares') - use the Geography page figure. STAGE B: figures disagree. vaticanstate.va and Britannica give 0.44 km2; Wikipedia gives 0.49 km2, citing the De Agostini Atlas Calendar (44 ha in the 1930 edition, corrected to 49 ha in 1945-46). The OSM boundary (relation 36989) measures 0.49 km2 geodesic (computed in stage_b/map/prep_geometry.py).

facts.text: Vatican City's boundary is formed by walls except on the St Peter's Square side, where a strip of travertine joins the outer ends of the colonnade.
The Leonine Walls were first built by Pope Leo IV (847-855).
facts.source_location: 'Leo IV (847-855) chose the same site ... to build the first walls of the civitas, which became known as Leonine'.
facts.uncertainty: Britannica says 9th century, completed under Leo IV. Most of today's boundary walls are later (16th-17th c.) - not yet sourced.

facts.text: The Holy See (the Pope and the central bodies of Church government) and Vatican City State are distinct international persons; diplomacy and treaties for both are conducted by the Pope through the Secretariat of State.
facts.source_location: 'Both the Holy See ... and Vatican City State, have always widely obtained full recognition of their distinct international personalities'; Fundamental Law 13 May 2023 Art. 6 quoted.
facts.uncertainty: Legal scholars debate the exact relationship (e.g. Göttingen Journal of International Law article: https://journals.uni-goettingen.de/gojil/article/download/2017/1712/4524 - not yet read in full).

facts.text: The Holy See became a Permanent Observer State at the UN on 6 April 1964; GA resolution 58/314 (1 July 2004) set out its participation rights.
facts.uncertainty: It is the Holy See, not Vatican City, that holds observer status. It cannot vote in the General Assembly (per UN guide - confirm wording).

facts.text: The Holy See has diplomatic relations with 184 states, plus the EU and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta (as of 9 January 2026).
facts.source_location: First sentence of the Informative Note.
facts.uncertainty: Number can change; re-check before publishing.

facts.text: Vatican City's form of government is an absolute monarchy; the Pope holds full legislative, executive and judicial power.
Vatican City is the smallest independent state in the world.
facts.source_location: History page: describes the State as the smallest in the world (see also the Geography page).
facts.uncertainty: Depends on counting only fully independent, recognised states (e.g. Sovereign Military Order of Malta has no territory).

facts.text: Porta Pia is on the north-east side of the Aurelian Walls; the 1870 breach was in the wall close to the gate, not through it.
facts.source_location: OSM node 2140602057 (historic=city_gate, name=Porta Pia) at 41.90932 N, 12.50132 E; walls = OSM ways named 'Mura Aureliane'.
facts.uncertainty: The breach's exact position (about 50 m west of the gate, by the modern Corso d'Italia) is not plotted because no verifiable coordinate has been sourced. The map labels the gate with 'breach nearby'.

facts.text: Map geometry is drawn from: the OSM Vatican boundary (relation 36989); OSM 'Mura Aureliane' and 'Mura gianicolensi' ways (surviving or mapped sections only, with gaps where demolished or unmapped); the OSM Tiber (relation 1827384); OSM buildings and Piazza San Pietro (relation 10044166); and Natural Earth 10m admin-0 for Italy and its neighbours.
facts.source_location: Overpass queries in stage_b/map_data/*.overpass (OSM base timestamp 2026-10-23T22:53Z); stage_b/map_data/ne_admin0_10m.geojson
facts.uncertainty: Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on Rome. Wall gaps reflect OSM coverage. Natural Earth 10m coastline is generalised.

facts.text: On-screen label 'Border marked by a strip of travertine paving' across St Peter's Square. The highlighted segment is the part of the OSM boundary inside the Piazza San Pietro polygon, about 125 m long, at the outer ends of the colonnades.
facts.source_location: Geography page paragraph on territory (see C24); segment computed in stage_b/map/prep_geometry.py
facts.uncertainty: The OSM line follows a slight arc. Not checked against Annex I of the Lateran Treaty map.

facts.text: Pius XI's decision to seek a general settlement was strongly motivated by the need to safeguard Catholic organisations (notably Catholic Action) as Fascism tightened its grip; the Church sought legal guarantees of its freedom and presence in Italian life.
facts.source_location: Pollard, The Vatican and Italian Fascism, 1929-32 (CUP, 1985/2010), ch. 5 extract: 'the Pope's decision to seek a general settlement ... was strongly motivated by the imperative need to safeguard the future of the Catholic organisations during the period of fascistisation'.
facts.corroboration: Treccani Dizionario di Storia, 'lateranensi, Patti': 'Con l'avvento del fascismo, la Chiesa si preoccupò di ottenere garanzie per la propria libertà e la propria presenza nella vita del Paese mediante strumenti giuridici, quindi nel 1926 furono avviate le trattative' (https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/patti-lateranensi_(Dizionario-di-Storia)/).
facts.uncertainty: Interpretation, not documented fact. Only the chapter extract (public abstract) was read, not the full book.

facts.text: For Mussolini, conducting the secret negotiations personally ensured the settlement would be acclaimed as his achievement alone; the final breakthrough came from his opportunistic policy towards the Church from 1921, though earlier governments (Nitti, Bonomi, 1919 onwards) had already negotiated key points.
facts.source_location: Pollard ch. 3 extract: 'For Mussolini, direct involvement in and responsibility for the negotiations ensured that it would be acclaimed as his achievement, and his alone.' Ch. 2 extract (https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511562945.002): historians agree the Conciliazione 'was far from being the work of Mussolini alone' ... 'the final breakthrough was due to the boldly opportunistic policy which Mussolini adopted towards the Church from 1921 onwards'; serious negotiations began in 1919.
facts.corroboration: Treccani 'lateranensi, Patti': negotiations opened in 1926; earlier attempts under Leo XIII failed.
facts.uncertainty: Interpretive; single academic author (well regarded) plus Treccani for chronology. Do not claim Mussolini's inner motives as fact.

facts.text: Treaty preamble: to assure the Holy See 'absolute and visible independence', it must be guaranteed an indisputable sovereignty even in the international field, hence the need to constitute Vatican City.
facts.source_location: Preamble: 'Che dovendosi, per assicurare alla Santa Sede l'assoluta e visibile indipendenza, garantirLe una sovranità indiscutibile pur nel campo internazionale, si è ravvisata la necessità di costituire ... la Città del Vaticano'
facts.corroboration: English (unofficial) translation spcp.prf.cuni.cz: 'absolute and visible independence of the Holy See, likewise to guarantee its indisputable sovereignty in the field of international relations'.
facts.uncertainty: Our English rendering. On screen, cite 'Lateran Treaty (1929), preamble'.

facts.text: The popes from 1870 to 1929: Pius IX (to 1878), Leo XIII (1878-1903), Pius X (1903-14), Benedict XV (1914-22), Pius XI (1922-39).
facts.source_location: List of Supreme Pontiffs, nos. 255-259 with dates.

facts.text: The 1929 agreements were written into the Italian Constitution of 1947 (in force 1948).
facts.source_location: 'Gli accordi raggiunti nel 1929 furono inseriti nella Costituzione italiana del 1947.'
facts.corroboration: Britannica Lateran Treaty: 'confirmed by the Italian constitution of 1948'.

facts.text: A monastic community existed at Westminster (Thorney) before Edward the Confessor; the Abbey dates a Benedictine monastery to about 960 under King Edgar and St Dunstan.
facts.source_location: 'St Edward's church': 'a small Benedictine monastery founded under the patronage of King Edgar and St Dunstan around 960A.D.'
facts.uncertainty: VCH (1909) treats the 785 Offa charter as possibly genuine (community before 785) and the Edgar/Dunstan restoration as 'highly probable', with early charters unreliable. Britannica says 'certain' about 785 - stronger than VCH.

facts.text: In the 1040s Edward the Confessor established his royal palace on Thorney Island by the Thames and re-endowed and greatly enlarged the monastery, building a large stone church dedicated to St Peter.
facts.corroboration: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/426/ (OUV: 'since Edward the Confessor built his palace and church on Thorney Island in the 11th century')
facts.uncertainty: Exact start date of building not given (usually c.1050s); keep to 'mid-eleventh century'.

facts.text: The church became known as the 'west minster', traditionally to distinguish it from St Paul's (the 'east minster') in the City of London.
facts.source_location: 'This church became known as the "west minster" to distinguish it from St Paul's Cathedral (the east minster)'.
facts.uncertainty: VCH quotes the Offa charter (785) already naming 'aet Westminster', so the name may be older than Edward's church; the east/west explanation is traditional.

facts.text: Edward's church was consecrated on 28 December 1065; the king was too ill to attend, died on the night of 4-5 January 1066 and was buried before the High Altar on 6 January 1066.
facts.source_location: 'consecrated on Holy Innocents' Day, 28th December 1065, but the king was ill and unable to be present' ; 'He died sometime on the night of 4-5th January 1066 ... buried on 6th'.
facts.uncertainty: Death date given as 5 January in many references; Abbey says night of 4-5 January.

facts.text: Edward's funeral procession to the Abbey is depicted on the Bayeux Tapestry.
facts.source_location: 'Burial and Shrine': 'The burial procession from Westminster Hall to the Abbey ... is depicted on the Bayeux Tapestry.'
facts.uncertainty: The Abbey says the procession started from 'Westminster Hall' - Westminster Hall itself was built 1097 (Parliament); read as 'the palace'. Tapestry images: use public-domain reproductions only and check photo licence.

facts.text: Harold Godwinson, Edward's successor, was probably crowned at Westminster (January 1066), but no surviving contemporary evidence confirms where.
facts.source_location: 'Early coronations': 'His immediate successor, Harold Godwinson, is likely to have been crowned here ... but there is no surviving contemporary evidence to confirm this ceremony.'
facts.uncertainty: DISPUTED/INCONSISTENT: the Abbey's own 2025 Annual Report states coronations have taken place 'since that of Harold II in 1066'. Its history page is the more careful statement.

facts.text: William the Conqueror was crowned at Westminster on Christmas Day 1066 - the first documented coronation there; Ealdred (Aldred), Archbishop of York, performed it in place of Stigand of Canterbury.
facts.source_location: 'Coronation': 'crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, according to the ancient English rite. Aldred, archbishop of York performed the ceremony in place of Stigand'.
facts.corroboration: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/coronations-at-the-abbey/a-history-of-coronations ('The first documented coronation at Westminster was that of William the Conqueror on 25th December 1066') ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Westminster-Abbey

facts.text: During William's coronation the congregation's shouted approval (in English and French) was mistaken by Norman soldiers outside for an attack; they set fire to nearby houses, most of the congregation fled, and the clergy completed the rite.
facts.source_location: 'When the French-speaking Normans and English-speaking Saxons then shouted their approval the Norman soldiers outside thought the noise inside was an assassination attempt and began setting fire to houses around the Abbey. Smoke filled the church and the congregation fled ... William and the officiating clergy completed the service despite the chaos.'
facts.uncertainty: Based on Norman-era chroniclers: William of Poitiers (contemporary, partisan) and Orderic Vitalis (writing decades later; source of 'the king trembling'). Abbey says 'assassination attempt'; Orderic/Thornbury say rising/alarm. Motives of soldiers are the chroniclers' reading.

facts.text: William probably chose Westminster to reinforce his claim to be Edward's legitimate successor.
facts.source_location: 'William probably chose the Abbey for his coronation to reinforce his claim to be a legitimate successor of Edward.'

facts.text: Before 1066 there was no fixed coronation place: Edward himself was crowned at Winchester (1042) and King Edgar's coronation was at Bath.
facts.source_location: 'Before this year there had been no fixed location for the ceremony.' ; 'coronation of Edgar ... at Bath Abbey'.
facts.uncertainty: Edgar's Bath coronation is usually dated 973 (History Press); Abbey page gives no year.

facts.text: Edward was canonised in 1161 (Pope Alexander III) and his body was translated to a new shrine on 13 October 1163.
facts.source_location: 'officially canonized as Saint and Confessor by Pope Alexander III in February 1161' ; 'On 13th October 1163, St Edward's body was transferred to a Shrine'.

facts.text: Henry III began demolishing Edward's church in 1245 and rebuilt it in the Gothic style; the new church was consecrated on 13 October 1269, when Edward's body was moved to Henry's new shrine.
facts.source_location: 'Demolition of Edward the Confessor's 11th century church began in 1245 ... consecration of the Church took place on 13th October 1269'.
facts.corroboration: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/history-of-westminster-abbey ; https://www.britannica.com/topic/Westminster-Abbey (1245; nave of Edward's church left standing)
facts.uncertainty: Britannica: Edward's nave survived for a time; Henry's work reached only one bay west of the screen - the old nave stood attached for many years.

facts.text: Henry III designed his church to be not only a monastery but a place for the coronation and burial of monarchs, with a coronation 'theatre' planned under the central lantern.
facts.source_location: 'Westminster Abbey was designed to be not only a great monastery and place of worship, but also a place for the coronation and burial of monarchs.'
facts.corroboration: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/coronations-at-the-abbey/a-history-of-coronations ('a large space or "theatre" was planned under the lantern')
facts.uncertainty: Henry's personal devotion to Edward is the other main motive (H3 page).

facts.text: Henry III's rebuilding including the shrine cost about £45,000.
facts.source_location: 'the cost including the new Shrine was £45,000, about 15 million in today's money'.

facts.text: Henry III was first crowned hastily at Gloucester on 28 October 1216 and then again with full ceremony at Westminster on 17 May 1220.
facts.corroboration: https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/london/vol1/pp433-457 ('17 May, 1220, a second coronation was performed in the abbey')
facts.uncertainty: EXCEPTION to 'every coronation since 1066 at Westminster': Henry III's first coronation was at Gloucester.

facts.text: Edward I (1274) was the first king crowned in the present Gothic church.
facts.source_location: 'The first king to be crowned in the present Abbey was Edward I in 1274.'

facts.text: Every monarch since William the Conqueror has been crowned in the Abbey except Edward V and Edward VIII, who were never crowned.
facts.source_location: 'Coronations and burials': 'Every monarch since William the Conqueror has been crowned in the Abbey, with the exception of Edward V and Edward VIII (who abdicated)'.
facts.uncertainty: Qualifiers: Harold uncertain (C06); Henry III also crowned at Gloucester (C15); Lady Jane Grey (1553) never crowned and her status as monarch is debated; William III and Mary II jointly crowned.

facts.text: King Charles III was the 40th reigning monarch to be crowned at the Abbey, on 6 May 2023.
facts.source_location: 'King Charles III was the 40th reigning monarch to be crowned in May 2023.'
facts.uncertainty: The count depends on conventions (Harold; joint monarchs). Attribute the number to the Abbey.

facts.text: Coronation arrangements are made by the Earl Marshal for the Crown; the Archbishop of Canterbury crowns the monarch; the Dean of Westminster instructs the sovereign on the service.
Since the late 14th century coronations have broadly followed the order in the Abbey's Liber Regalis manuscript.
facts.source_location: 'every coronation ceremony has basically followed the same order of service laid down in ... the Liber Regalis'.
facts.uncertainty: 'Basically' - the rite has changed (English from 1603, new elements 1953 and 2023).

facts.text: The anointing, done under a canopy, is regarded as the most sacred part of the coronation, rather than the crowning.
facts.source_location: 'The Anointing': 'this, and not the crowning, is the most sacred part of the service'.
facts.uncertainty: Religious framing - present as the Church's view.

facts.text: Edward I took the Stone of Scone from Scotland to Westminster in 1296 and had an oak chair made (1300-1301) to contain it - the Coronation Chair, painted by Master Walter (Walter of Durham).
facts.corroboration: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/coronations-at-the-abbey/spotlight-on-coronations/coronation-chair ; https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-news/stone-of-destiny-welcomed-to-the-abbey ; https://perthmuseum.co.uk/the-stone-of-destiny/ ('Taken as war loot by King Edward I')

facts.text: The Coronation Chair has been used at coronations since 1308 (Edward II) and certainly for the crowning since 1399 (Henry IV); the Abbey says 26 monarchs have been crowned on it since 1308.
facts.source_location: 'Since the coronation of King Edward II in 1308, 26 monarchs have been crowned on this chair.'
facts.corroboration: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/explore-our-history/the-coronation-chair ('opinion is divided as to when it was actually used for the crowning, but this was certainly the case from 1399')
facts.uncertainty: Abbey pages differ in certainty; Mary I used a different chair (CHAIR).

facts.text: The Stone of Destiny was used for inaugurating Scottish kings at Scone; its first documented use was for Alexander III in 1249.
facts.source_location: 'Its first documented use was in 1249 for the inauguration of the boy-king, Alexander III.'
facts.uncertainty: Legendary origins (Jacob's pillow, Tara, Lia Fail) are legends; HES analysis says the sandstone is consistent with the Scone Sandstone Formation (https://www.historicenvironment.scot/about-us/news/research-shines-new-light-on-the-stone-of-destiny/).

facts.text: On 3 July 1996 the Prime Minister John Major announced the Stone's return to Scotland; it left the Abbey on 13-14 November 1996, was displayed at Edinburgh Castle, and since 2024 has been at Perth Museum; it returns to Westminster for coronations.
facts.corroboration: https://blog.historicenvironment.scot/2023/05/the-story-of-the-stone-of-destiny/ ; https://perthmuseum.co.uk/the-stone-of-destiny/ ('arrived shortly before the Museum opened in March 2024')

facts.text: The Stone was brought back to the Abbey for Charles III's coronation (welcomed at a service on 29 April 2023); the King sat in the Coronation Chair for the anointing, investiture and crowning on 6 May 2023.
facts.corroboration: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/coronations-at-the-abbey/spotlight-on-coronations/coronation-chair ('The King sat in the Coronation Chair for ... the Anointing, the Investiture and the Crowning')

facts.text: At the 2023 service the Homage of Peers was replaced by a 'Homage of the People'; Welsh, Scottish Gaelic and Irish Gaelic were used; girl choristers and female bishops took part for the first time.
facts.uncertainty: Homage of the People attracted public debate in 2023 - not sourced here; do not characterise reactions.

facts.text: Westminster Abbey is neither a cathedral nor a parish church but a 'Royal Peculiar' (the Collegiate Church of St Peter), under a Dean and Chapter and subject only to the Sovereign, not to any archbishop or bishop.
facts.uncertainty: Britannica says 'under the jurisdiction of the British monarch and not the Church of England' - misleading (it is a Church of England church). Do not use that wording.

facts.text: The Abbey's exemption from the Bishop of London long predates the Reformation: after a claim by Bishop Eustace in 1221, arbitrators in 1222 found for the abbey.
facts.source_location: Pp. 433-457, section on exemption: 'the archbishop of Canterbury and the other arbitrators of 1222 were justified in pronouncing in favour of the abbey'.
facts.uncertainty: Medieval exemption was papal/monastic; 'Royal Peculiar' in the modern sense dates from the Tudor period (Abbey: from 1534; charter 1560).

facts.text: Henry VIII dissolved the monastery on 16 January 1540 and later that year made Westminster a cathedral with its own bishop, Thomas Thirlby; the last abbot, William Boston, became dean.
facts.source_location: 'dissolution of the medieval monastery on 16th January 1540. The same year Henry VIII erected Westminster into a cathedral church with a bishop, Thomas Thirlby'.
facts.corroboration: https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/london/vol1/pp433-457 ('his convent was dissolved on 16 January, 1540 ... in the following December the new cathedral church was erected, Abbot Boston being appointed dean')

facts.text: The bishopric of Westminster was surrendered on 29 March 1550 and the diocese reunited with London - Westminster's ten years as a cathedral with its own bishop.
facts.source_location: 'The bishopric was surrendered on 29th March 1550 and the diocese was re-united with London'.
facts.uncertainty: Abbey adds it remained 'a cathedral church in the diocese of London' by Act of Parliament until Mary's restoration - nuance.

facts.text: Mary I restored Benedictine monks under Abbot John Feckenham in November 1556; under Elizabeth I the monks were removed in July 1559.
facts.source_location: 'Mary I restored the Benedictine monastery in 1556 under Abbot John Feckenham' ; 'the Abbot and monks were removed in July 1559'.

facts.text: Elizabeth I's charter of 21 May 1560 refounded the Abbey as a Collegiate Church exempt from archbishops and bishops, with the Sovereign as Visitor; its staff included the scholars who formed the nucleus of Westminster School.
Members of the Dean and Chapter are appointed by the Crown and answer to the King; the Abbey receives no funding from the Church Commissioners, the State or the Crown.
facts.source_location: 'Status of the Abbey' / 'Governance and management' sections.

facts.text: The Commons first met in the Abbey's Chapter House in 1352 and moved to the Abbey's Refectory in 1397; from 1547 Edward VI gave them St Stephen's Chapel in the Palace, used until the 1834 fire.
facts.corroboration: https://www.parliament.uk/about/living-heritage/evolutionofparliament/originsofparliament/birthofparliament/keydates/1215to1399/ ; https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/explore-our-history/chapter-house ('the House of Commons met here for a few years in the 14th century')
facts.uncertainty: Parliament's own pages give 1547 (meeting places) and 1548 (St Stephen's page). The Abbey says 'a few years'; Parliament gives 1352-1397 but sessions were intermittent and the Commons also used other rooms (Hawkyard, Parliamentary History 2002).

facts.text: The Chapter House was built c.1246-c.1255, is octagonal (about 18 m across inside); the King's Great Council met there in 1257, which the Abbey calls 'effectively the beginning of the English Parliament'.
facts.uncertainty: DISPUTED framing: Parliament dates the term 'Parliament' to 1236 and highlights 1265 (de Montfort) and 1295. 'Beginning of Parliament' is the Abbey's interpretation.

facts.text: After 1540 the Chapter House was used as a repository for State records until 1863.
Westminster Hall (built 1097) is the oldest building on the Parliamentary estate; Parliament, the law courts and government offices grew up around it.
facts.source_location: Intro paragraph and 'Events and other uses'.
facts.uncertainty: Parliament's 'meeting places' page notes the Hall itself was not used for parliamentary meetings.

facts.text: The Palace of Westminster, Westminster Abbey and St Margaret's Church form one UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 1987), described as symbolising monarchy, religion and power since Edward the Confessor.
facts.source_location: 'Outstanding Universal Value' and inscription details (1987; criteria i, ii, iv).

facts.text: Thirty royals are buried in the Abbey (13 kings, 4 queens regnant, 11 queens consort, 2 other queens); the last monarch buried there was George II in 1760.
Henry VII's Lady Chapel was consecrated on 19 February 1516; Elizabeth I's coffin lies on top of Mary I's in its vault.

Chaucer was the first poet buried in what became Poets' Corner (1400), because he was Clerk of the King's Works; Spenser was later buried near him; more than 100 poets and writers are buried or memorialised there, chosen by the Dean.
facts.uncertainty: Spenser's dates: Abbey gives '1553-1598' but he died January 1599 (1598 Old Style) - avoid year on air.

facts.text: The Unknown Warrior was buried at the west end of the nave on 11 November 1920 in the presence of King George V, brought from France; the idea came from the chaplain David Railton and was carried out by Dean Herbert Ryle.
facts.source_location: Opening paragraphs; 'How was the Unknown Warrior selected?'.
facts.uncertainty: Britannica says the remains were 'brought from Flanders (Belgium)' - contradicts the Abbey and the grave inscription ('BROUGHT FROM FRANCE'). Selection from four battle areas (Abbey: 'some sources say six').

facts.text: The grave is covered by black Belgian marble (1921) and is the only gravestone in the Abbey that people may not walk on; the inscription ends 'They buried him among the kings ...'.
facts.source_location: Inscription text and 'Who is the Unknown Warrior?' paragraph.
facts.uncertainty: The inscription is a primary text displayed in the Abbey; quoting a line is fine (1920s public inscription, not a modern translation).

facts.text: Since 1923 royal brides married at the Abbey have laid their bouquets on the Unknown Warrior's grave; Queen Camilla's coronation bouquet was laid there in 2023.
facts.source_location: 'New stone and the Congressional Medal' section.

facts.text: Sixteen royal weddings have taken place at the Abbey, beginning with Henry I in 1100; Princess Elizabeth married there on 20 November 1947 and was crowned there on 2 June 1953.
Queen Elizabeth II's State funeral took place at the Abbey on 19 September 2022; she was buried at St George's Chapel, Windsor.
The western towers were completed in 1745 to a design by Nicholas Hawksmoor (with John James).
facts.source_location: 'Two centuries later a further addition ... western towers ... completed in 1745, to a design by Nicholas Hawksmoor.'
facts.uncertainty: VISUAL ACCURACY: the familiar twin towers did not exist before 1745 - must not appear in any medieval or Tudor reconstruction.

facts.text: Pope Benedict XVI became the first pope to visit the Abbey, in 2010.
facts.source_location: 'In 2010 His Holiness Pope Benedict XVI became the first Pope to visit the Abbey.'

facts.text: Photography in the Abbey: video recording is not permitted; professional photography needs Press Office approval; photography is never allowed in the Shrine, St Faith's Chapel or the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries.
facts.uncertainty: Policy can change - re-check before Stage C.

facts.text: On Christmas Day 1950 four University of Glasgow students, Scottish nationalists, removed the Stone from the Abbey; it was recovered in April 1951.
facts.source_location: '1950: An unexpected removal' section ('four University of Glasgow students (and Scottish Nationalists)')
facts.corroboration: https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/explore-our-history/the-coronation-chair ('stolen by Scottish Nationalists on 25th December 1950. After its recovery in April 1951...')
facts.uncertainty: None on the facts. Tone: describe neutrally; no judgement of the students.

facts.text: On 16 October 1834 fire destroyed most of the old Palace of Westminster.
facts.source_location: Key dates: '1834 - The Great Fire destroys most of Palace ... 16 October'

facts.text: Exchequer tally sticks were notched wooden receipts for money paid to the Crown, originating in the Middle Ages; split in two, the halves were 'married up' to confirm payment.
facts.source_location: Tally sticks page + Great Fire page 'Did you know?' ('Split in two ... the parts were married up again')
facts.uncertainty: Wood species varies by source: HC hazel; Dickens says elm (rhetoric). Say 'wooden' or 'hazel or willow'

facts.text: The tally system was abolished in 1826 (parliament.uk: 'not been used since 1826'), leaving about two cart-loads of old tallies.
facts.source_location: 'two cart-loads of wooden tally sticks ... not been used since 1826'
facts.uncertainty: Legal abolition 1782/1826 nuances; keep to 1826 per parliament.uk

facts.text: The Clerk of Works chose to burn them in the two underfloor stoves (furnaces) beneath the House of Lords rather than on a bonfire or give them away as firewood.
facts.source_location: 'the Clerk of Works thought that the two underfloor stoves in the basement of the House of Lords would be a safe and proper place'

facts.text: With so much fuel fed into them, the underfloor furnaces burned very hot; a chimney fire smouldered in the flues under the floor during the day. (Stage A's 'designed to burn coal, not wood' was DROPPED: single secondary chain only.)
facts.source_location: 'The furnaces burned incredibly hot with so much fuel being fed into them, and this eventually led to the floor of the House of Lords catching fire'
facts.corroboration: History of Parliament Online, 'The fire of 1834' (chimney fire smouldering under the floor); parliament.uk Great Fire page (heat of the floor, smoke)
facts.uncertainty: Coal-design claim (Wikipedia citing Shenton 2012) not independently verified - removed from narration

facts.text: Two labourers, Joshua Cross and Patrick Furlong, fed the tallies into the furnaces from the morning of 16 October.
facts.source_location: 'two Irish labourers, Joshua Cross and Patrick Furlong, were assigned the task' (Shenton)
facts.corroboration: Spectator 22 Nov 1834 parody names 'Josh Cross'; parliament.uk says 'a couple of workmen'
facts.uncertainty: Spectator 25 Oct 1834 (closed-door reports) named 'James Scott' -> early press confusion

facts.text: In the afternoon, visitors shown round the Lords by the deputy housekeeper Mrs Wright were puzzled by the heat of the floor and smoke seeping through it, but the work continued.
facts.source_location: 'a party of visitors ... conducted by the deputy housekeeper Mrs Wright, became puzzled by the heat of the floor, and by the smoke seeping through it. But the workmen insisted on finishing'
facts.corroboration: HC ('Housekeeper and the Clerk of Works ... noticed excess smoke and heat ... but did not put them out'); Wikipedia (heat through boots)
facts.uncertainty: Title varies: 'deputy housekeeper' (parl.uk) vs 'Housekeeper' (Spectator, HC); first name not established in our sources

facts.text: The furnaces were out by about 5pm and Mrs Wright locked up; at about 6pm a doorkeeper's wife raised the alarm that the Lords was on fire.
facts.source_location: 'The furnaces were put out by 5pm ... At 6pm, Mrs Wright heard the terrified wife of a doorkeeper screaming that the House of Lords was on fire'
facts.corroboration: HC ('a doorkeeper's wife raised the alarm'); Wikipedia (first flames 6pm)
facts.uncertainty: Wikipedia: workers left shortly after 4pm; timings approximate

facts.text: By 6.30pm a fireball had burst through the roof.
facts.source_location: 'By 6.30pm on 16 October 1834, a huge fireball had exploded through the roof'

facts.text: The flames spread quickly through the palace's timber-and-plaster interiors, driven by the wind; parliament.uk had long-standing warnings (1789 architects' report incl. Soane and Adam; Soane again 1828).
facts.source_location: 'In 1789, a report signed by fourteen architects, including John Soane and Robert Adam ... In 1828, John Soane again drew attention to the fire risk ... timber covered with plaster'
facts.uncertainty: Wind direction detail from Wikipedia only

facts.text: James Braidwood's London Fire Engine Establishment attended with 12 engines and 64 firemen although the palace was uninsured government property; low tide hampered pumping.
facts.source_location: London Fire Brigade Museum (Braidwood): 'alongside 64 firefighters and 12 fire engines'; London Museum broadsheet, object 484467: 'Twelve fire engines, 64 firefighters'
facts.corroboration: Wikipedia (Shenton); heritagecollections.parliament.uk (LFEE, parish engines, low tide)
facts.uncertainty: Numbers now verified by two independent sources

facts.text: Thousands watched from the streets, bridges and boats; soldiers held the crowds back; the glow was visible from Windsor, about 20 miles away.
facts.source_location: 'Thousands of people gathered ... from ... boats on the River Thames ... The King and Queen could see it from Windsor Castle, around 20 miles away'
facts.corroboration: GF ('kept back by soldiers'); DF ('thousands of other sightseers'); PMA catalogue says 'tens of thousands'

facts.text: J. M. W. Turner watched and painted the fire, including two oils now in Cleveland and Philadelphia; Constable and probably Dickens also witnessed it.
facts.source_location: 'Turner and Constable, and probably Dickens, witnessed the fire'
facts.corroboration: GF (Turner 'painted several canvases'); CMA 1942.647; PMA M1928-1-41

facts.text: Barry and Pugin, the future architects, both watched the old palace burn; Pugin wrote that it was 'a glorious sight'.
facts.source_location: 'By chance, both men had watched the old Palace burn down' + Pugin letter 6 Nov 1834 quoted
facts.uncertainty: Pugin's quote is about Soane's/Wyatt's additions burning, not glee at the disaster as a whole

facts.text: Efforts concentrated on saving Westminster Hall; the Prime Minister, Lord Melbourne, directed efforts to douse the roof.
facts.source_location: 'The Prime Minister, Lord Melbourne, quickly directed efforts to douse the roof'
facts.corroboration: HC ('Firefighters now focused on Westminster Hall'); Wikipedia (Melbourne in crowd)
facts.uncertainty: Who 'directed' is disputed in tone; Braidwood/firemen did the work

facts.text: The Chancellor of the Exchequer reportedly cried 'Damn the House of Commons, let it blaze away! Save, O save, the Hall!'
facts.source_location: 'The Chancellor of the Exchequer reportedly declared: "Damn the House of Commons, let it blaze away! Save, O save, the Hall!"'
facts.corroboration: BBC 2009 names Lord Althorp (Chancellor of the Exchequer in Oct 1834)

facts.text: Westminster Hall was saved by firefighting (the tide turned, a floating engine pumped from the river, scaffolding gave access to the roof) and a change of wind around midnight.
facts.source_location: 'First, the tide turned ... floating barge mounted fire engine ... around midnight ... change in wind direction ... scaffolding inside Westminster Hall'
facts.corroboration: GF ('heroic fire fighting efforts, and a change in the direction of the wind'); WH page

facts.text: Survivors: Westminster Hall, the Undercroft Chapel (St Mary Undercroft, the crypt), the Cloisters and Chapter House of St Stephen's, and the Jewel Tower (whose stored records survived).
facts.source_location: 'The only other parts of the Palace to survive were the Jewel Tower, the Undercroft Chapel, the Cloisters and Chapter House of St Stephen's and Westminster Hall'
facts.corroboration: DF (wind away from Jewel Tower, records preserved); English Heritage; HC (crypt damaged by heat and smoke)
facts.uncertainty: Lists differ slightly; Jewel Tower stands apart from today's palace (English Heritage)

facts.text: Lost: both chambers - the Commons (in St Stephen's Chapel, its home since 1547-48) and the Lords - plus the Painted Chamber, the Speaker's House and most Commons records.
facts.source_location: 'Most of the Palace had been lost, including both the House of Lords and the House of Commons Chambers' ; Commons/Lords temporarily used the Lords and the Painted Chamber shell
facts.corroboration: parliament.uk St Stephen's pages (1547-48); Wikipedia (Painted Chamber destroyed; Commons records lost; Lords' Journals survived in Jewel Tower)
facts.uncertainty: Painted Chamber: HC says the Lords moved into its shell -> it was gutted, not erased

facts.text: No one died; the fire crews left five days later.
facts.source_location: 'no one died in the disaster' ; 'The fire crews finally left five days after'
facts.corroboration: Wikipedia ('no deaths, although there were nine casualties')

facts.text: A Privy Council inquiry found the burning of the tallies was the cause, acquitted everyone of deliberate intent, called it 'unaccountable' that Mrs Wright took no precaution and regretted that the Clerk of Works had not supervised more closely; no one was prosecuted.
facts.source_location: 'unanimous opinion that the burning of the Exchequer tallies was the original cause ... acquit all parties of guilty design ... "unaccountable" that Mrs. Wright ... regret that Mr. Weobly ... had not paid greater attention'
facts.corroboration: HC ('No one was prosecuted, although a public inquiry found various people guilty of negligence and foolishness'); Wikipedia (sat from 22 Oct)
facts.uncertainty: Blame is shared/diffuse; do not single out the labourers

facts.text: Rumours of arson and foreknowledge (e.g. a Mr Cooper's claim that the fire was talked of in Dudley before it started) were investigated and discredited.
facts.source_location: Spectator 25 Oct 1834 reports Cooper's Dudley story; 22 Nov: the Council 'utterly discredit Mr. Cooper's testimony'
facts.corroboration: Wikipedia (other theories: plumbers, Howard's Coffee House, gas)

facts.text: A newspaper parody of the report, 'the house that Josh burnt', went the rounds of the daily papers.
facts.source_location: 'afforded a fair subject for the following rather clever parody ... This is the house that Josh burnt'

facts.text: The damage to the uninsured palace was estimated at £2 million.
facts.source_location: 'The damage to the wrecked and uninsured Palace was estimated at £2 million'

facts.text: In June 1835 the Royal Commission required the new building to be Gothic or Elizabethan; neo-classical was associated with revolution and republicanism, Gothic with conservative values.
facts.source_location: 'as the design was associated with revolution and republicanism while the Gothic style was felt to embody conservative values, the commission announced in June 1835 that the style ... should either be Gothic or Elizabethan'
facts.corroboration: Key dates; Designing a New Palace page
facts.uncertainty: Interpretation of 'meaning' is parliament.uk's; keep as 'was felt to'

facts.text: The 1836 competition drew 97 entries identified by pseudonym or symbol; the commissioners unanimously preferred no. 64, marked with a portcullis: Charles Barry's.
facts.source_location: 'They received 97 entries ... unanimous in preferring entry number 64 which bore the emblem of the Portcullis'
facts.uncertainty: Key dates page says '1835' competition (announced 1835, judged 1836)

facts.text: Barry employed the young Gothic specialist A. W. N. Pugin on the competition drawings and later the interiors; Pugin designed most of the Gothic interior detail.
facts.source_location: 'Pugin ... paid £400 by Barry ... it was Pugin who designed most of the Palace's sumptuous Gothic interiors'
facts.corroboration: HC architects story (Pugin invited 1844 for interiors)
facts.uncertainty: Credit disputes between the two men's families later - don't adjudicate

facts.text: Construction began in 1840; Lords chamber completed 1847, Commons 1852; Barry estimated six years, it took over 30 and cost over £2 million; finished c.1870, a decade after Barry's death, by his son Edward.
facts.source_location: 'Barry estimated a construction time of six years ... took more than 30 years, at a cost of over £2 million'; key dates 1847/1852/1870
facts.corroboration: AR ('not until 10 years after Barry's death in 1860')

facts.text: The clock tower grew under Pugin's influence; the Great Clock started 31 May 1859 and the second Great Bell, 'Big Ben', first struck on 11 July 1859; the tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
facts.source_location: 'began keeping time on 31 May 1859 ... Big Ben rang out for the first time on 11 July 1859'
facts.corroboration: BB key-dates page; designing-a-new-palace page (Pugin's influence); how-the-clock-tower-has-changed (25 June 2012)
facts.uncertainty: Name 'Big Ben' popularly = tower; strictly the bell; naming after Sir Benjamin Hall is 'believed'/'probably'

facts.text: UNESCO: the Abbey inspired Barry and Pugin's work, and the Palace, the clock tower and Big Ben's sound are 'internationally recognised symbols of Britain and democracy'.
facts.corroboration: Inscribed 1987 together with Westminster Abbey and St Margaret's

facts.text: Dickens (speech, 27 June 1855) used the tally fire as a parable of official routine: 'The stove, overgorged with these preposterous sticks, set fire to the panelling; the panelling set fire to the House of Lords; the House of Lords set fire to the House of Commons; the two houses were reduced to ashes'.
facts.source_location: Dickens Search transcription; identical wording in Speeches Literary and Social (fulltextarchive)
facts.corroboration: https://www.fulltextarchive.com/book/Speeches-Literary-and-Social/2/ (wording of this sentence identical; other parts differ: '1843' vs '1834', 'build two more' vs 'build others')
facts.uncertainty: HC presents it as 'remarked after the fire' (actually 21 years later) and abridges it; Dickens calls the tallies 'elm'

facts.text: Florence Cathedral was founded in 1296; Brunelleschi's dome was built 1420-1436 and is still the largest masonry vault in the world; a 45.5 m octagonal dome had been planned since 1367 with no agreed way to build it.
facts.source_location: 'built between 1420 and 1436 ... still the largest masonry vault in the world ... planned since the 1300s'
facts.corroboration: Opera magazine posts (founded 1296; 1367 project, 45.5 m; work began 7 Aug 1420; completed 30 Aug 1436)
facts.uncertainty: 'Unfinished because nobody knew how to build the dome' simplifies: nave/drum work also took time

facts.text: It was the biggest fire London had seen since the Great Fire of 1666.
facts.source_location: 'The scale of the fire was enormous - the biggest in London since the Great Fire of 1666.'
facts.corroboration: Shenton (via Wikipedia): 'the most momentous blaze in London between the Great Fire of 1666 and the Blitz'
facts.uncertainty: Earlier draft attributed a 'most significant ... Blitz' wording to Shenton; that exact wording could not be verified, so the line was rewritten to the parliament.uk wording

facts.text: Hundreds of volunteers helped to work the pumps and were paid in beer.
facts.source_location: 'Hundreds of volunteers helped, including MPs and Peers. Those who staffed the water pumps on the night ... were given beer tokens for their efforts.'
facts.corroboration: History of Parliament Online, 'The fire of 1834' (volunteers paid in beer)
facts.uncertainty: 'Beer tokens' - narration simplifies to 'paid in beer'

facts.text: The new cathedral was begun in 1296 to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio, replacing Santa Reparata.
facts.source_location: Opera magazine 1420 post: founded 1296, designed by Arnolfo di Cambio
facts.corroboration: https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/la-sfida-della-cupola_(Il-Contributo-italiano-alla-storia-del-Pensiero:-Tecnica)/ (Arnolfo laid first stone 1296, then S. Reparata)
facts.uncertainty: Whether Arnolfo planned a dome of this size: 'not all historians agree' (Opera)

facts.text: In 1367 a model by Neri di Fioravanti (and a committee) was chosen over Giovanni di Lapo Ghini's; it fixed an octagonal dome about 45.5 m across.
facts.source_location: 1367 experts' project fixed the octagon and 45.5 m span
facts.uncertainty: Columbia summary (search only) says the choice went to a citizens' referendum; names of the committee vary

facts.text: The 1367 design fixed size and shape but not how to build it.
facts.source_location: 'didn't give any details of what construction techniques'

facts.text: The interior span is about 45.5 m; external diameter about 55 m.
facts.source_location: Dome page: 45.5 m interior, 55 m external
facts.uncertainty: Measurements differ by method (octagon flat-to-flat vs corner)

facts.text: From 1367 the cathedral's officials swore an oath to follow the approved model.
facts.source_location: 3 Sep 1425: 'modellum cupole dicte ecclesie vigens prosequi et non aliud'
facts.uncertainty: NatGeo says 'every year'; the 1425 record is an oath on entering office (terms were short). Start date 1367 per NatGeo

facts.text: 'Half a century': 1367 model to 1418 competition (51 years) / 1420 start (53 years).
facts.source_location: 1367 project; competitions ended 16 Apr 1420; worksite opened 7 Aug 1420
facts.uncertainty: Drum only finished c.1413–17, so urgency came late; Opera funded studies meanwhile

facts.text: On 19 Aug 1418 the Opera announced a competition for models or designs for the dome's vault and its centring/scaffolds, with a prize of 200 gold florins.
facts.source_location: AOSMF II 1 74 c.9v: 'tam pro armadura quam pro pontibus'; 200 florins; proclaimed 20 Aug

facts.text: Brunelleschi trained as a goldsmith and lost the 1401 Baptistery doors competition to Lorenzo Ghiberti.
facts.source_location: Britannica: goldsmith; 1401 contest won by Ghiberti

facts.text: Much of what we know of Brunelleschi's life comes from Antonio Manetti's biography of the 1480s, written decades after the events.
facts.uncertainty: Manetti was an admirer; details are not contemporary

facts.text: Brunelleschi is said to have studied Roman ruins with Donatello after 1401.
facts.uncertainty: Source is Manetti/Vasari; dating and length uncertain

facts.text: Vasari tells that Brunelleschi won over the judges by standing an egg on end — 'so it is said'.
facts.source_location: Vasari, Life of Brunelleschi (Gutenberg 25759 l.~5807): 'so it is said, there arose the dispute about the egg'
facts.uncertainty: LEGEND. Vasari wrote c.130 years later; Manetti reportedly omits it; similar tale later told of Columbus (Benzoni 1565) and earlier variants exist (Pacioli/Filicaia, https://revistas.ucm.es/index.php/CFIT/en/article/download/60872/4564456552434/4564456576592)

facts.text: Vasari also relates proposals to fill the crossing with earth mixed with coins, and that Brunelleschi was carried out as 'mad'.
facts.uncertainty: ANECDOTE; not in the Opera documents

facts.text: On 16 Apr 1420 Brunelleschi, Ghiberti and Battista d'Antonio were put in charge of the dome; Brunelleschi and Ghiberti were paid 3 florins a month.
facts.uncertainty: Opera magazine also says Brunelleschi was 'elected Superintendent' on 7 Aug 1420 — conflict; use 16 Apr / 'in 1420'

facts.text: Ghiberti remained joint supervisor for years; he was reconfirmed with Brunelleschi in 1431.
facts.uncertainty: Vasari's hostile portrait (feigned illness trick) is ANECDOTE

facts.text: Brunelleschi's 1420 programme: two shells, ribs, stone and timber chains; built without centring up to 30 braccia, then 'senz'alcuna armadura'.
facts.source_location: Treccani citing Brunelleschi, Documento-programma 1420 (Di Pasquale 2002 pp.87–88)
facts.corroboration: Britannica Florence Cathedral; UCI Becker page (search only)
facts.uncertainty: The programme is known through later copies; text editions vary

facts.text: Construction began 7 Aug 1420, marked with a celebratory meal for the workers.
The dome has two shells, an inner thicker one and an outer one, linked by ribs; stairs run between them.
facts.source_location: two domes; 24 meridian, 10 parallel ribs; 463 steps
facts.uncertainty: Rib counts described differently (8 corner + 16 intermediate)

facts.text: It was built without a full wooden centring (a timber frame supporting the vault).
facts.uncertainty: Working platforms were used. Britannica's 'no scaffolding' phrasing is wrong; avoid

facts.text: Herringbone (spinapesce): upright bricks set at intervals tie each new course to the one below so incomplete rings stay stable.
facts.source_location: Treccani: spinapesce connects bricks of the advancing ring to the previous ring while the new ring is incomplete
facts.uncertainty: DEBATED: exact function and layout reconstructed (Jones, Sereni & Ricci, JSAH 2010 https://online.ucpress.edu/jsah/article/69/1/39/92442/Building-Brunelleschi-s-Dome-A-Practical; other hypotheses)

facts.text: Brick courses tilt increasingly inward towards the top; their alignment was controlled from the centre (e.g. with cords).
facts.corroboration: Britannica Florence Cathedral ('measuring wires fixed at the centers of curvature'); Treccani
facts.uncertainty: DEBATED: exact geometry (conical beds, loxodromes) contested

facts.text: Rings of sandstone with iron cramps and a ring of oak beams were built in to resist spreading.
facts.source_location: Britannica: stone chains with metal cramps; timber rings

facts.text: The dome weighs an estimated 37,000 tonnes and contains perhaps more than four million bricks.
facts.source_location: 'estimated 37,000 metric tons'; bricks 'may exceed four million'
facts.corroboration: Opera magazine: 29,000 t lifted; Treccani: 30 million kg lifted
facts.uncertainty: Figures measure different things and are estimates

facts.text: Brunelleschi designed an ox-driven hoist whose load could be reversed without turning the oxen round.
facts.source_location: Museo Galileo: c.1420; pair of oxen; three speeds; reversal without unhitching
facts.uncertainty: Exact design known from later drawings (Taccola, Leonardo, Buonaccorso Ghiberti)

facts.text: In 1421 the Opera paid for lifting with 'one or two oxen' on Filippo's machine.
facts.source_location: 31 Mar 1421 'con l'aiuto di uno o due buoi all'edificio di Filippo'

facts.text: In 1421 Florence granted Brunelleschi a three-year privilege for a new boat to carry goods (marble) on the Arno.
facts.uncertainty: Often called the 'first patent'; Kostylo: 'by no means the first'

facts.text: The boat (later nicknamed 'Il Badalone') is reported to have failed around 1428.
In August 1434 Brunelleschi was arrested at the instance of the masters' guild for not paying its fee; the Opera ordered the guild's consuls arrested.
facts.source_location: 20 Aug 1434: consuls 'fecerunt capi … Filippum indebite et iniuste … non solvit matriculam'
facts.uncertainty: Length of detention not in this record (often given as ~11 days)

facts.text: Brunelleschi warned against sharing inventions with many (reported by the engineer Taccola).
facts.source_location: Kostylo citing Prager (1968) on Taccola's report
facts.uncertainty: Reported speech, not Brunelleschi's own text; translation

facts.text: No document survives in which Brunelleschi explains his whole method.
facts.source_location: 'no documentation survives that explicitly explains his engineering'

facts.text: Pope Eugenius IV consecrated the cathedral on 25 March 1436.
facts.source_location: 13 Mar 1436: preparations for consecration 'per summum pontificem die viginti quinque martii 1436'
facts.uncertainty: Opera magazine says Eugene consecrated 'the Dome' on 30 Aug 1436 — conflict

facts.text: The dome itself was closed at the top on 30 August 1436.
facts.source_location: 'On 30 August 1436 the work on Brunelleschi's dome was completed'
facts.uncertainty: Blessing that day often attributed to the Bishop of Fiesole (search only)

facts.text: Alberti praised the dome as able to cover 'all the Tuscan people' with its shadow, built without wooden supports.
facts.source_location: NatGeo quote of Alberti, De pictura dedication

facts.text: The lantern was designed by Brunelleschi but finished after his death; Verrocchio's gilded ball was placed in 1471.
facts.source_location: Dome page: lantern; ball 1471; current ball early-1600s replacement

facts.text: Brunelleschi died in 1446 and was buried in the cathedral; his tomb was found in 1972.
It is still the largest masonry dome in the world (claim by the Opera).
facts.source_location: 'still the largest masonry vault in the world'
facts.uncertainty: Superlative depends on definition; the Pantheon (concrete) spans ~43.3 m (Treccani)

facts.text: An imagined dome already appears in Andrea di Bonaiuto's Spanish Chapel fresco (1365–67), before anyone knew how to build it.
facts.uncertainty: Fresco shows an idealised design, not Neri's model

facts.text: Ep05 bridge: the Illuminati were founded in 1776 at Ingolstadt by the canon-law professor Adam Weishaupt; banned in Bavaria 1784–85.
facts.uncertainty: Founding date 1 May 1776 widely given; myth far exceeds history

facts.text: Bridge: no historical connection between Brunelleschi and the Illuminati is implied; the link is thematic (secrecy).
The drum (tambour) was completed c.1410-13; the dome springs about 54 m (Moore: 175 ft) above the cathedral floor.
facts.source_location: sgira: drum completed by 1410-13; Moore 1905 ch.2: 'springing level is a hundred and seventy-five feet above the pavement'
facts.uncertainty: Exact completion year of drum varies by source (1410-1413); height figures vary 52-55 m

facts.text: The 1420 programme says the outer shell protects the inner from damp and makes it more magnificent; build without centring to 30 braccia, then decide, 'because in building, practice teaches what is to be followed'.
facts.source_location: Moore 1905 ch.2 quoting Guasti 1857 pp.28-30: '...perchè nel murare la pratica insegna quello che si ha da seguire'
facts.corroboration: Guasti, La cupola di Santa Maria del Fiore (1857), pp.28-30 (PD)
facts.uncertainty: Translation ours; programme text is commonly attributed to Brunelleschi (with the other supervisors)

facts.text: A secret society, later called the Order of the Illuminati, was founded in Ingolstadt, Bavaria, on 1 May 1776 by Adam Weishaupt.
facts.source_location: 'Founded in 1776 by the young professor of canon law Adam Weishaupt (1748-1830) at the University of Ingolstadt'
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) ('founded on May Day 1776'); https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Illuminati; https://germanhistory-intersections.org/en/knowledge-and-education/ghis:document-190
facts.uncertainty: Gotha dates the order '1776/78 to 1787/88'; 1 May is the traditional founding date (Britannica, 1911 EB, WDR 2021)

facts.text: The order existed for only about a decade (to c. 1787/88).
facts.source_location: 'existed from 1776/78 to 1787/88'; 'only existed for a good decade (according to current knowledge until 1787)'
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) (no record of activity after 1785)

facts.text: Weishaupt was born in Ingolstadt in 1748 and educated by the Jesuits.
facts.source: https://www.freemasonry.bcy.ca/texts/illuminati.html (T. W. McKeown, 'A Bavarian Illuminati Primer', Grand Lodge of BC&Y)
facts.source_location: 'born February 6, 1748 at Ingolstadt and educated by the Jesuits'
facts.corroboration: https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit (1748-1830); https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) ('former Jesuit' – i.e. Jesuit-trained)
facts.uncertainty: Britannica's 'former Jesuit' is loose; he was Jesuit-educated, not a Jesuit priest

facts.text: In his twenties Weishaupt held the chair of canon law at Ingolstadt, previously held by Jesuits.
facts.source: https://www.freemasonry.bcy.ca/texts/illuminati.html (T. W. McKeown, 'A Bavarian Illuminati Primer', Grand Lodge of BC&Y)
facts.source_location: appointment as Professor of Natural and Canon Law in 1775, 'a position previously held by one of the recently disbanded Jesuits'
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972) (professor 1773); https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit ('young professor of canon law')

facts.text: Pope Clement XIV dissolved the Jesuit order in 1773, but ex-Jesuits remained influential in Bavaria and at Ingolstadt.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: 'Jesuits, whose order Pope Clement XIV had dissolved in 1773 … still retained the purse strings and some power at the university'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (university 'fast vollständig von ehemaligen Jesuiten beherrscht')

facts.text: The order was a product of the Enlightenment: its aims were education, reason and moral improvement, opposed to clerical influence and abuse of power.
facts.source_location: Mulsow's FAZ article (listed): originally 'the project of a religiously founded Enlightenment'
facts.corroboration: https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20171127-the-birthplace-of-the-illuminati ('formed to oppose religious influence on society and the abuse of power by the state'); https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) ('republican free thought'; 'religion of reason')
facts.uncertainty: Historians differ on how radical the aims were ('radically enlightened or even early democratic' – Gotha summary of 1980s research)
