facts.text: Weishaupt saw secrecy as protection for spreading Enlightenment ideas under censorship.
facts.source_location: Jefferson: 'as Wishaupt lived under the tyranny of a despot & priests, he knew that caution was necessary'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (protection from Jesuit intrigues; access to banned literature); https://germanhistory-intersections.org/en/knowledge-and-education/ghis:document-190
facts.uncertainty: Interpretive; Jefferson relied on Barruel's quotations

facts.text: The founding group first called themselves the Perfectibilists.
The owl of Minerva was the society's emblem.
facts.source_location: 'Als Symbol des Bundes wählte er die Eule der Minerva' (citing Agethen 1987)
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972) (Minerval degree emblem: owl on a book)
facts.uncertainty: Secondary only; fits the 'Minerval' grade name (Britannica)

facts.text: Members used code names; Weishaupt was 'Spartacus'; Munich was 'Athens' and Ingolstadt 'Eleusis'.
facts.source_location: 'Weishaupt selbst nannte sich nach dem Anführer des antiken Sklavenaufstands Spartacus … München hieß z. B. Athen … Ingolstadt Eleusis'
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972) (Munich (Athens), Ingolstadt (Eleusis), citing Le Forestier 1914); https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit (Goethe's order name via Gotha research)
facts.uncertainty: Secondary sources; Stage C: confirm city names in the 1787 Originalschriften

facts.text: By 1778 the group was renamed the Order of the Illuminati and had a couple of dozen members.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: 'In April 1778, the order became the Illuminatenorden'; 'By the end of summer 1778 the order had 27 members'
facts.corroboration: https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit (Perfectibilists 'until 1778'); https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (about 60 members by 1780)

facts.text: Members advanced through graded classes, with aims disclosed step by step, and kept watch on one another.
facts.source_location: 'kept internal discipline and a system of mutual surveillance'; three classes from novices to 'magus' and 'king'
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Illuminati; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972) ('a system of mutual espionage')
facts.uncertainty: Higher 'mysteries' grades probably never fully written (ENW)

facts.text: Weishaupt joined a Munich Masonic lodge in 1777; Illuminati then took control of a Munich lodge (Theodor zum guten Rat).
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: admitted to lodge 'Prudence' Feb 1777; Lodge Theodore founded Munich 21 Mar 1779 and 'quickly packed with Illuminati'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) ('1777 gelang die Unterwanderung zweier Münchner Freimaurerlogen'); https://www.freemasonry.bcy.ca/texts/illuminati.html (T. W. McKeown, 'A Bavarian Illuminati Primer', Grand Lodge of BC&Y)
facts.uncertainty: Details of which lodge differ (McKeown names Theodore for 1777)

facts.text: Adolph Knigge, a Protestant baron and Freemason from the Hanover area, was recruited in 1780.
facts.source_location: 'am 1. Juli 1780 in der Loge L'Union in Frankfurt … geworben'
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972) (recruited late 1780 by Costanzo); https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit (Knigge 'played a decisive role in the expansion of the order from 1780 onwards')

facts.text: Weishaupt admitted to Knigge that the order's ancient superiors/antiquity were fictions and the higher grades not yet written; Knigge wrote them.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: 'In January 1781 … Weishaupt finally confessed that his superiors and the supposed antiquity of the order were fictions and the higher degrees had yet to be written' (Le Forestier)
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (by Weishaupt's own admission the order existed 'only in his head'; Knigge gave it its grade structure in 1782)
facts.uncertainty: Secondary; letters edited in Markner et al. 2005 (Korrespondenz)

facts.text: Knigge targeted lodge masters, so whole lodges joined; after the Wilhelmsbad convent (1782) the order spread through German lands and into Austria.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: 'He targeted the masters and wardens … able to place the entire lodge at the disposal of the Illuminati'; expansion after Wilhelmsbad (16 Jul 1782)
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (Wilhelmsbad 16 Jul–1 Sep 1782); https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) (area 'from Italy to Denmark and from Warsaw to Paris')

facts.text: Goethe joined the order in 1783; Duke Ernst II of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg was a member and patron.
facts.source_location: 'Goethe, who had become a member of the Order in 1783'; Bode ran the Thuringian branch 'under the patronage of Duke Ernst II of Gotha'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (Ernst II joined end of Jan 1783); https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) (says such notables were 'claimed as members although it is questionable')
facts.uncertainty: Britannica doubts some famous memberships; Gotha (primary-archive research) confirms Goethe and Ernst II

facts.text: Membership estimates reach about 2,500, though far fewer members can be identified by name.
facts.source: Michael Barkun, A Culture of Conspiracy, 2nd ed., University of California Press 2013 (local copy research/barkun_culture_of_conspiracy_2013.pdf)
facts.source_location: pp. 47–48: 'By the early 1780s, it had acquired a peak membership of approximately twenty-five hundred, most in German-speaking areas.'
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) ('at no time, however, do its numbers appear to have exceeded 2,000'); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972) (about 650 verifiable by end 1784; FactGrid)
facts.uncertainty: Estimates vary (c. 650 named to c. 2,500 claimed)

facts.text: Knigge left the order in July 1784 after quarrels with Weishaupt.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: 'In July 1784 Knigge left the order by agreement'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (Weimar 'Congress' Feb 1784 to settle the dispute); https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) ('internal dissension')

facts.text: Indiscretion made the order's existence widely known; it was accused of placing members in government bodies.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: 'loose talk … caused the "secret" order's existence to become common knowledge'; Illuminati in many civic bodies
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Geschichte_des_Illuminaten-Ordens/Die_Ordensverfolgung_in_Bayern (L. Engel 1906, reprints the edicts verbatim) (16 Aug 1785 edict: Illuminati in justice colleges, 'die Oberhand und Mehrheit der Stimmen')
facts.uncertainty: The edict's charge is the government's claim

facts.text: On 22 June 1784 Elector Karl Theodor banned all societies formed without official approval.
facts.source: https://www.digitale-sammlungen.de/de/view/bsb10935405?page=3 (BSB print of the 22 June 1784 edict, PD scan)
facts.source_location: Printed edict 'München den 22. Juny 1784' against 'Communitäten, Gesellschaften und Verbrüderungen' without approval (scan p. 3)
facts.corroboration: https://www.digitale-sammlungen.de/de/view/bsb00098194 (BSB print of the 2 March 1785 edict, PD scan; catalogue says 'Ausstellungsdatum 21. März' but the print reads 'den 2ten März 1785', header '2. Merz 1785') (refers back to the ban 'unterm 22sten Juny letztverwichenen Jahrs'); https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Geschichte_des_Illuminaten-Ordens/Die_Ordensverfolgung_in_Bayern (L. Engel 1906, reprints the edicts verbatim)

facts.text: The edict of 2 March 1785 named Freemasons and Illuminati, banned their meetings, collections and recruiting, declared collected money forfeit and promised half to the informer.
facts.source: https://www.digitale-sammlungen.de/de/view/bsb00098194 (BSB print of the 2 March 1785 edict, PD scan; catalogue says 'Ausstellungsdatum 21. März' but the print reads 'den 2ten März 1785', header '2. Merz 1785')
facts.source_location: '…Logen der sogenannten Freymaurer und Illuminaten…'; 'verbiethen derselben all weitere Conventicula, anmaßliche Kollekten, und Anwerbungen neuer Mitglieder'; 'Geld und Gut, deklariren Wir für confiscabel … die Hälfte der armen Cassa, die andere Hälfte aber dem Aufbringer, wenn er gleich selbst ein Mitglied wäre'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Geschichte_des_Illuminaten-Ordens/Die_Ordensverfolgung_in_Bayern (L. Engel 1906, reprints the edicts verbatim) (same text reprinted)

facts.text: Weishaupt lost his chair, fled to Regensburg and later to Gotha, under Duke Ernst II's protection; he died in 1830.
facts.source_location: 'Weishaupt, had to flee Ingolstadt and initially found refuge in Regensburg, then from 1787 in Gotha'
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) ('stripped of his chair at Ingolstadt and banished'); https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (Ernst gave him a sinecure as Hofrat)
facts.uncertainty: McKeown wrongly places his later career at Göttingen; Gotha is correct

facts.text: The 'courier struck by lightning' story is widely retold with varying details.
facts.source: https://www.freemasonry.bcy.ca/texts/illuminati.html (T. W. McKeown, 'A Bavarian Illuminati Primer', Grand Lodge of BC&Y)
facts.source_location: 'Retellings of the death of Lanz, an Illuminati courier, who was struck by lightning in Regensburg illustrate the mythology … sometimes been imaginative in the details'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (papers found on a deceased courier revealed some names)
facts.uncertainty: Some papers may have come from a dead courier; the lightning detail is unverified by us

facts.text: Zwack's house in Landshut was searched on 11–12 October 1786 and Illuminati papers were seized.
facts.source: https://archive.org/details/einigeoriginalsc01duke_0 (Einige Originalschriften des Illuminatenordens, Munich: Strobel 1787; DDB record https://www.deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de/item/HPM7HA2GK2VQ5AVEVGO4T2KD57UY26UR)
facts.source_location: Title: '…welche bey dem gewesenen Regierungsrath Zwack durch vorgenommene Hausvisitation zu Landshut den 11. und 12. Octob. 1786 vorgefunden worden'
facts.corroboration: https://www.freemasonry.bcy.ca/texts/illuminati.html (T. W. McKeown, 'A Bavarian Illuminati Primer', Grand Lodge of BC&Y) (11 Oct 1786)

facts.text: Baron Bassus's castle at Sandersdorf was also searched and further papers published.
facts.source_location: Title: 'Nachtrag von weitern Originalschriften … bey der auf dem Baron Bassusischen Schloß zu Sandersdorf … vorgenommenen Visitation entdeckt'
facts.corroboration: https://www.freemasonry.bcy.ca/texts/illuminati.html (T. W. McKeown, 'A Bavarian Illuminati Primer', Grand Lodge of BC&Y) (16 Oct 1786)

facts.text: The Bavarian government printed the seized papers in 1787 as 'Einige Originalschriften des Illuminatenordens' ('Some Original Writings…').
facts.source: https://archive.org/details/einigeoriginalsc01duke_0 (Einige Originalschriften des Illuminatenordens, Munich: Strobel 1787; DDB record https://www.deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de/item/HPM7HA2GK2VQ5AVEVGO4T2KD57UY26UR)
facts.source_location: Title: '…auf höchsten Befehl Seiner Churfürstlichen Durchleucht zum Druck befördert' (archive.org metadata); imprint Munich: Strobel, 1787 (DDB record)
facts.corroboration: https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit ('confiscated during house searches and subsequently published in printed form'); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)

facts.text: Historians regard the popular image of an all-powerful order as resting on legend rather than evidence; the papers show a small, quarrelsome reform society.
facts.source_location: 'this widespread assumption is based less on historically verifiable facts and findings than on legends and conspiracy theories'
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) ('After 1785 the historical record contains no further activities'); https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (Stubley: 'eher einer extra-curricularen studentischen Lerngruppe … als einer Dissidentenzelle')

facts.text: Jefferson (31 Jan 1800) called Barruel's own parts 'the ravings of a Bedlamite' and judged Weishaupt an 'enthusiastic Philanthropist'.
facts.source_location: 'Barruel's own parts of the book are perfectly the ravings of a Bedlamite'; 'Wishaupt seems to be an enthusiastic Philanthropist'
facts.corroboration: Papers of Thomas Jefferson vol. 31 (Princeton UP), print edition of the same letter

facts.text: The French Revolution began in 1789; conservatives looked for a hidden cause.
facts.source_location: the conspiracy legends 'essentially arose in the temporal context of the French Revolution itself'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (Barruel/Robison blamed the Illuminati rather than Enlightenment ideals, the bad harvest, Louis XVI's crisis management)

facts.text: Barruel, an exiled French ex-Jesuit priest, published 'Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire du Jacobinisme' from 1797 (English: 'Memoirs Illustrating the History of Jacobinism', London 1797-98).
facts.source: https://archive.org/search?query=creator%3ABarruel+AND+title%3Amemoirs (e.g. archive.org/details/memoirsillustrat04barr; Barruel, Memoirs Illustrating the History of Jacobinism, Eng. tr. 1797-98)
facts.source_location: English translation volumes dated 1797-99 in archive.org catalogue
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972) (1797-98; 'a Jesuit exiled from France'); https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975)

facts.text: John Robison, professor of natural philosophy at Edinburgh, published 'Proofs of a Conspiracy' in 1797.
facts.source: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/47605 (Robison, Proofs of a Conspiracy, Edinburgh 1797)
facts.source_location: Full title: 'Proofs of a conspiracy against all the religions and governments of Europe, carried on in the secret meetings of Free Masons, Illuminati, and reading societies' (Edinburgh 1797)
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dictionary_of_National_Biography,_1885-1900/Robison,_John (professor of natural philosophy, Edinburgh, from 1773; RSE general secretary)

facts.text: Barruel and Robison (independently) claimed the Illuminati survived the ban and, through Masonic lodges, helped cause the French Revolution.
facts.source_location: claims that the Illuminati 'had instigated the French Freemasons to instigate the revolution in France'
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972) ('publicised the theory that the Illuminati had survived … behind the French Revolution'); https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) ('unabhängig voneinander')
facts.uncertainty: These are their claims; no supporting evidence

facts.text: Bode's 1787 visit to Paris was cited as evidence; he won over only a few French Freemasons.
facts.source_location: 'Bode was only able to win over a few French Freemasons … probably the starting point for the claim … that the Illuminati had instigated the French Freemasons'
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) (stayed 24 Jun–17 Aug 1787; invited to a Masonic convent already over when he arrived)

facts.text: No document shows the Illuminati directing the French Revolution.
facts.source_location: 'After 1785 the historical record contains no further activities of Weishaupt's illuminati'
facts.corroboration: https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit (popular view 'based less on historically verifiable facts … than on legends'); https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) ('Dieser Verschwörungsthese fehlte also jede Grundlage')

facts.text: In 1798 New England clergy (e.g. Jedidiah Morse, Fast Day sermon of 9 May 1798) warned of an Illuminati conspiracy.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: 'one of the first accounts of the Illuminati to be printed in the United States was Morse's Fast Day sermon of 9 May 1798' (citing Stauffer 1918; Fraser 2018)
facts.corroboration: https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Jefferson/01-31-02-0297 ('illuminati Morse' as he is now called)

facts.text: Washington wrote (24 Oct 1798) that he did not believe American lodges, as societies, had spread Illuminati doctrines, while believing the doctrines had reached the US.
facts.source_location: 'I did not believe that the Lodges of Free Masons in this Country had, as Societies, endeavoured to propagate the diabolical tenets of the first'; 'It was not my intention to doubt that, the Doctrines of the Illuminati … had not spread in the United States'
facts.corroboration: Mount Vernon catalogue (ALS); NOI PDF transcription

facts.text: In the twentieth century, writers such as Nesta Webster bound the Illuminati myth to antisemitic conspiracy theories.
facts.source: Michael Barkun, A Culture of Conspiracy, 2nd ed., University of California Press 2013 (local copy research/barkun_culture_of_conspiracy_2013.pdf)
facts.source_location: pp. 48–50: Webster and Lady Queenborough 'added … that Jews were central to these activities'; Gerald Winrod (1935) and the Protocols linked to the Illuminati
facts.corroboration: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminatenorden (secondary; cites Markner/Neugebauer-Wölk/Schüttler 2005, Agethen 1987, van Dülmen 1975) ('Die anti-illuminatische Verschwörungstheorie wurde Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts antisemitisch aufgeladen'); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)

facts.text: The 'Illuminatus!' trilogy (1975) by Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson was satire that helped popularise the modern myth.
facts.source_location: Wilson 'and another Playboy writer wrote The Illuminatus! Trilogy'; began as Discordian satire
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Illuminatus!_Trilogy (Dell, 1975)
facts.uncertainty: BBC overstates in saying the myth 'started' in the 1960s – it began in the 1790s

facts.text: The pyramid and eye come from the reverse of the US Great Seal, adopted 20 June 1782.
facts.source_location: 'on June 20, 1782, the seal was officially adopted by the Continental Congress'
facts.corroboration: https://diplomacy.state.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/Great-Seal-PDF.pdf (Thomson retained the pyramid with the Eye of Providence)

facts.text: The Eye of Providence was a conventional symbol of divine oversight; the MDCCLXXVI on the pyramid marks 1776, American independence.
facts.source_location: '13-step pyramid with the year 1776 in Roman numerals on the base … heralding the beginning of the new American era in 1776'
facts.corroboration: https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20201112-the-eye-of-providence-the-symbol-with-a-secret-meaning ('a conventional symbol for God's sympathetic oversight')

facts.text: The Great Seal design was added to the $1 note in 1935.
facts.source_location: 'In 1935, President Roosevelt received a new design for the one-dollar bill … featured both sides of the Great Seal'

facts.text: Modern groups using the Illuminati name have no demonstrated link to the Bavarian order.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972)
facts.source_location: 'there is no evidence that these present-day groups have any real connection to the historic order' (citing McKeown 2009)
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/illuminati (read via archive.ph/ECIbw; local copy research/britannica_archive_illuminati.txt) (no record after 1785)

facts.text: Summary thesis: the order was real but small and short-lived; its posthumous legend far outgrew it.
facts.source_location: 'most notorious secret society of all time' although it 'only existed for a good decade' and 'barely exceeded the borders of the Holy Roman Empire'
facts.uncertainty: Editorial framing ('the order's enemies did more to make it immortal') is our interpretation

facts.text: The Illuminati recruited heavily from Freemasonry, which still exists and meets openly today (bridge to ep06).
facts.source_location: Order's Masonic links; Gotha lodge history to 1793/1801
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminati (secondary; cites Le Forestier 1914, Schüttler 1991, Roberts 1972); UGLE https://www.ugle.org.uk/ (Stage A for ep06 to source)

facts.text: In ep05 the Illuminati recruited through Masonic lodges; when the order was crushed, writers blamed the lodges too.
facts.source: Cornerstone History ep05 claims.csv (C13, C16, C34, C36, C38; sources: Gotha Research Centre Illuminati unit https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit ; Britannica 'Illuminati')
facts.source_location: ep05 C13/C16 (lodge recruitment), C34 (Barruel and Robison 1797 blamed Illuminati working through lodges)

facts.text: Britannica calls Freemasonry the world's largest secret society, while noting members do not necessarily conceal membership.
facts.source_location: 'the largest worldwide secret society' … membership not necessarily concealed
facts.uncertainty: 'Secret society' is contested by Masons, who prefer 'society with secrets'

facts.text: Medieval masons built cathedrals and castles; 'lodge' first meant a workshop on a building site (first mention Vale Royal Abbey, 1278).
facts.source_location: 'The original use of the word lodge indicates a workshop erected on the site of a major work, the first mention being Vale Royal Abbey in 1278.'
facts.corroboration: https://www.ugle.org.uk/discover-freemasonry/history-freemasonry (UGLE's own account; research/ugle_webfetch.txt) (consensus: origins lie with medieval stonemasons who built castles and cathedrals)

facts.text: The craft grades were apprentice, fellow of the craft and master; Masonic degrees derive from them.
facts.source_location: 'The degrees of Freemasonry are the three grades of medieval craft guilds: Entered Apprentice, Journeyman or Fellow of the craft, and Master Mason.'

facts.text: The Regius Poem (c. 1390–1425) is the oldest surviving document of its kind (the Old Charges); it says the craft came to England under King Athelstan.
facts.source_location: 'The Halliwell Manuscript, also known as the Regius Poem, is the earliest of the Old Charges'; 'brought to England during the reign of King Athelstan (924–939)'
facts.uncertainty: Dating range; Athelstan story is legendary

facts.text: On 28 December 1598 William Schaw, Master of Work to James VI and General Warden, issued statutes for all master masons in Scotland.
facts.source: First Schaw Statute, Edinburgh 28 Dec 1598, transcription https://archive.org/details/FirstSchawStatuteOf1598 (local research/schaw_1598_ia.txt); original in the minute book of the Lodge of Edinburgh (Mary's Chapel) No. 1
facts.source_location: 'At Edinburgh the XXVIII day of December … Sett doun be Williame Schaw, Maister of Wark, to his maiestie And generall Wardene of the said craft'
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Schaw (secondary; cites Stevenson, The Origins of Freemasonry: Scotland's Century 1590–1710, CUP 1988)

facts.text: The first statute required masons to be 'trew ane to ane vther and leve cheritablie togidder as becumis sworne brether and companzeounis of craft'.
facts.source: First Schaw Statute, Edinburgh 28 Dec 1598, transcription https://archive.org/details/FirstSchawStatuteOf1598 (local research/schaw_1598_ia.txt); original in the minute book of the Lodge of Edinburgh (Mary's Chapel) No. 1
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Schaw (secondary; cites Stevenson, The Origins of Freemasonry: Scotland's Century 1590–1710, CUP 1988) (modern-spelling version)
facts.uncertainty: On-screen original spelling; narration paraphrases in modern English

facts.text: The Second Schaw Statutes (28 Dec 1599) ranked Edinburgh, Kilwinning and Stirling and required lodges to keep written records via a notary.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Schaw (secondary; cites Stevenson, The Origins of Freemasonry: Scotland's Century 1590–1710, CUP 1988)
facts.source_location: 'Edinburgh Lodge would be most important followed by Kilwinning and then Stirling'; rules for record keeping
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Freemasonry (secondary; local research/wiki_history_freemasonry.txt) ('the 1599 directive that the lodges should employ a reputable notary as secretary')

facts.text: The first recorded admission of non-operative members was at the Lodge of Edinburgh on 3 July 1634.
facts.source_location: 'The first recorded admission of non-masons was on 3 July 1634 at Lodge of Edinburgh (Mary's Chapel)'
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Schaw (secondary; cites Stevenson, The Origins of Freemasonry: Scotland's Century 1590–1710, CUP 1988) (Stevenson)

facts.text: Elias Ashmole's diary, 16 Oct 1646: 'I was made a Free Mason at Warrington in Lancashire'.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Ashmole (secondary; quotes Ashmole's diary, Bodleian MS Ashmole 1136)
facts.corroboration: https://www.ugle.org.uk/discover-freemasonry/history-freemasonry (UGLE's own account; research/ugle_webfetch.txt) ('the first recorded evidence of the initiation of an English speculative mason')

facts.text: Traditional account: on 24 June 1717 four London lodges met at the Goose and Gridiron in St Paul's Churchyard, formed a Grand Lodge and elected Anthony Sayer.
facts.source_location: 'On St John's Day, 24 June 1717, four London Lodges … Goose and Gridiron … elected Anthony Sayer as their first Grand Master.'

facts.text: The 1717 account was first published in Anderson's 1738 Constitutions; no contemporary source mentions it; Anderson was not present.
facts.source: Prescott & Sommers, 'Searching for the Apple Tree: Revisiting the Earliest Years of Organised English Freemasonry', REHMLAC+ 9.2 (2018) 22–49, doi:10.15517/rehmlac.v9i2.31500; eprints.gla.ac.uk/130243 (local research/prescott_sommers_apple_tree.txt)
facts.source_location: 1717 story depends on Anderson 1738; 1723 edition silent; 'Anderson only became involved with Grand Lodge after June 1721'
facts.corroboration: Prescott & Sommers, '1717 and All That', https://www.quatuorcoronati.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/1717-And-All-That-Prescott-Sommers.pdf; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_Grand_Lodge_of_England (secondary; research/wiki_premier_gl.txt)

facts.text: Prescott & Sommers argue Grand Lodge took shape on 24 June 1721, when the Duke of Montagu was installed and the press first reported it.
facts.source: Prescott & Sommers, 'Searching for the Apple Tree: Revisiting the Earliest Years of Organised English Freemasonry', REHMLAC+ 9.2 (2018) 22–49, doi:10.15517/rehmlac.v9i2.31500; eprints.gla.ac.uk/130243 (local research/prescott_sommers_apple_tree.txt)
facts.source_location: earliest press reports June 1721 of the feast at which Montagu was installed Grand Master (Post Boy; Weekly Journal 1 July 1721)
facts.corroboration: J. Anderson, The Constitutions of the Free-Masons (London, 1723), PD scan https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Constitutions_of_the_Free_masons_(1723).pdf (local episode/archive/constitutions_1723.pdf) (General Regulations: Montagu chosen at Stationers' Hall, St John Baptist's Day 1721)

facts.text: In 1723 Grand Lodge published The Constitutions of the Free-Masons, compiled by James Anderson.
facts.source: J. Anderson, The Constitutions of the Free-Masons (London, 1723), PD scan https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Constitutions_of_the_Free_masons_(1723).pdf (local episode/archive/constitutions_1723.pdf)

facts.text: Its history traced masonry to Adam, Noah, Moses and Solomon's Temple.
facts.source: J. Anderson, The Constitutions of the Free-Masons (London, 1723), PD scan https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Constitutions_of_the_Free_masons_(1723).pdf (local episode/archive/constitutions_1723.pdf)
facts.corroboration: https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/libraryscience/25 (UNL edition of 1734 reprint: history 'from Adam to … George I')

facts.text: Charge I: 'A Mason is oblig'd by his Tenure, to obey the moral Law' … 'that Religion in which all Men agree, leaving their particular Opinions to themselves'.
facts.source: J. Anderson, The Constitutions of the Free-Masons (London, 1723), PD scan https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Constitutions_of_the_Free_masons_(1723).pdf (local episode/archive/constitutions_1723.pdf)

facts.text: Charge II: a Mason is 'never to be concern'd in Plots and Conspiracies against the Peace and Welfare of the Nation'.
facts.source: J. Anderson, The Constitutions of the Free-Masons (London, 1723), PD scan https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Constitutions_of_the_Free_masons_(1723).pdf (local episode/archive/constitutions_1723.pdf)

facts.text: Lodges confer three degrees: Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft, Master Mason.
The third degree appeared between 1723 and 1730; Prichard's 1730 exposure Masonry Dissected first shows the three degrees.
facts.source_location: 'In Pritchard's Masonry Dissected, an exposure … 1730 … something recognisable as the three degrees'; 'the third degree emerged sometime between 1723 and 1730'

facts.text: Ritual is an allegory centred on King Solomon's Temple and its architect Hiram Abiff.
facts.source_location: 'the internal allegory of masonic ritual, centred on King Solomon's Temple and its architect, Hiram Abiff'

facts.text: Square and compasses are the best-known Masonic emblem; builders' tools used to teach lessons in conduct.
facts.source_location: 'the single most identifiable symbol of Freemasonry'; 'used in Masonic ritual as emblems to teach symbolic lessons'

facts.text: Medieval masons used signs, grips and words; modern Masons use them as modes of recognition.
facts.source_location: medieval masons used grips, words and signs; aprons and gloves

facts.text: Grand Lodge of Ireland by 1725; Grand Lodge of Scotland 1736.
Franklin reprinted Anderson's Constitutions in Philadelphia in 1734, the first Masonic book printed in America, and signed as Grand Master of Pennsylvania.
facts.source: https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-01-02-0117 (Franklin to Henry Price, 28 Nov 1734, and editorial note 4)
facts.source_location: signed 'B. Franklin, G.M. Pennsylvania'; note 4 'Re-printed in Philadelphia by special Order'

facts.text: Washington was initiated an Entered Apprentice at Fredericksburg, Virginia, on 4 Nov 1752, aged 20.
facts.source_location: 'He was 20 years old when he received the first degree of Entered Apprentice on November 4, 1752.'

facts.text: Mozart was initiated into Vienna's lodge Zur Wohltätigkeit on 14 Dec 1784 and composed for lodge meetings.
facts.source_location: 'Als Mozart am 14. Dezember 1784 … als „Lehrling" in die Wiener Loge „Zur Wohltätigkeit" aufgenommen wurde'; works 'speziell für die Versammlungen des Bundes komponiert'

facts.text: Voltaire was initiated in 1778 at Les Neuf Sœurs in Paris, with Franklin among his conductors.
facts.source_location: 'Voltaire … Initiated on April [1778] in Paris; his conductors were Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Court de Gébelin'

facts.text: Pope Clement XII's bull In eminenti (28 April 1738) forbade Catholics to join, under pain of automatic excommunication.
facts.source_location: 'under pain of excommunication … incurred by the very deed'

facts.text: The bull's reasoning: 'For if they were not doing evil they would not have so great a hatred of the light.'
The 1983 CDF declaration, signed by Cardinal Ratzinger, confirmed Catholic membership remains forbidden.
facts.source_location: 'the Church's negative judgment in regard to Masonic association remains unchanged … membership in them remains forbidden'; signed Joseph Card. Ratzinger, 26 Nov 1983

facts.text: In 1826 William Morgan of Batavia, NY, a bricklayer, prepared a book revealing Masonic rituals; he was jailed on petty charges in September and vanished.
facts.source_location: 'ignited in 1826 by the mysterious disappearance of William Morgan, a bricklayer in western New York who supposedly had broken his vow of secrecy'

facts.text: Several Masons were convicted for kidnapping Morgan; his murder was never proved.
facts.source_location: Sheriff Eli Bruce 'convicted of conspiracy for his role in kidnapping Morgan'; Lawson, Chesebro, Sawyer convicted

facts.text: The Anti-Masonic Party was America's first third party and held the first national nominating convention (Baltimore, Sept 1831).
facts.source_location: 'It was the first American third party, the first political party to hold a national nominating convention'

facts.text: Its candidate William Wirt, himself a former Mason, carried only Vermont in 1832; the party then declined.
facts.source_location: 'Wirt won only the state of Vermont (seven electoral votes) in the 1832 election'

facts.text: The Soviet Union outlawed Freemasonry in 1922; Mussolini dissolved Italian Freemasonry in 1925.
facts.source_location: 'The Soviet Union definitively outlawed Freemasonry in 1922'; 'in 1925, he dissolved Freemasonry in Italy'

facts.text: Nazi Germany pressed lodges to 'voluntarily' dissolve, declared them hostile to the state (Oct 1934) and ordered all remaining lodges dissolved in Aug 1935, seizing assets.
facts.source_location: Göring decree 1934; Frick decree 28 Oct 1934 'hostile to the state'; 17 Aug 1935 all remaining lodges dissolved and assets confiscated

facts.text: Nazi propaganda alleged a 'Jewish-Masonic' conspiracy; the SD had a section devoted to Freemasonry; anti-Masonic exhibitions were held in occupied Paris (1940) and Brussels (1941).
facts.source_location: Section II/111; exhibitions Paris Oct 1940, Brussels Feb 1941

facts.text: Franco outlawed Freemasonry in Spain on 2 March 1940.
facts.source_location: 'Freemasonry was officially outlawed in Spain on 2 March 1940'

facts.text: Totalitarian regimes would not tolerate a private society they did not control (our interpretation).
facts.source_location: SD believed Freemasonry 'exercised actual political power'

facts.text: The Illuminati were real and recruited in lodges but were crushed in the 1780s; no document shows them (or Masons) directing the French Revolution.
facts.source: Cornerstone History ep05 claims.csv (C13, C16, C34, C36, C38; sources: Gotha Research Centre Illuminati unit https://www.uni-erfurt.de/en/gotha-research-centre/research/working-groups-and-networks/illuminati-research-unit ; Britannica 'Illuminati')

facts.text: Ramsay's 1737 Discourse linked Freemasonry to crusader knights (the Hospitallers), not explicitly the Templars.
facts.source_location: 'connected Freemasonry with the Knights Hospitaller'; 'erroneously … that Ramsay mentioned the Knights Templar'
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Freemasonry (secondary; local research/wiki_history_freemasonry.txt) ('the 1737 lecture of Chevalier Ramsay added the crusaders to the lineage')

facts.text: Von Hund's Strict Observance (named so after 1764) introduced the claim that Masons were heirs of the Templars.
facts.source_location: 'the Knights Templar became involved in the myth, starting with Karl Gotthelf von Hund's Rite of Strict Observance'
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Templars (research/britannica_templars_webfetch.txt) ('In the 18th century the Freemasons claimed … a secret line of succession')

facts.text: At Wilhelmsbad in 1782 the system's own delegates found 'only traditions and probabilities' and renounced the claim to be the Templars' legitimate successors.
facts.source: Recès du Convent de Wilhelmsbad (1782), art. II, https://www.directoirerectifiedefrance.org/reces-du-convent-de-wilhelmsbad-1782-regime-rectifie-et-ordre-du-temple/ (local research/wilhelmsbad_reces_1782.htm; notes research/wilhelmsbad_notes.txt)
facts.source_location: art. II: 'ne présentaient que des traditions et des probabilités sans titres authentiques … pas autorisés … à nous dire les vrais et légitimes successeurs des Templiers'
facts.corroboration: Aktenedition Wilhelmsbader Konvent (e-bookshelf PDF): 'die Templerlegende aufgegeben'
facts.uncertainty: They kept a chivalric form and a sense of affinity (art. III)

facts.text: Historians find no evidence of continuity from the medieval Templars to Freemasonry; Masonic Templar orders are later creations.
facts.source: Historia da Historiografia 20 (2016), doi:10.15848/hh.v0i20.940 (citing D. Harrison 2014: no proof, no link)
facts.corroboration: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Templar_legends (secondary; research/wiki_templar_legends.txt) ('connection is rejected by Masonic authorities themselves'); https://www.britannica.com/topic/Templars (research/britannica_templars_webfetch.txt)

facts.text: P2 was a covert lodge, dissolved by the Grand Orient in 1974 but run in secret by Licio Gelli; its member lists (politicians, magistrates, officers) were exposed in 1981; banned 1982.
facts.source_location: 'Sciolta nel 1974 ma ricostituita come associazione segreta nel 1975, sotto la guida di L. Gelli'; 'pubblicazione (1981) degli elenchi'; 'Sciolta d'autorità … (1982)'

facts.text: Verdict: no evidence of a single hidden Masonic hand running governments; abuses like P2 were individual and exposed (our conclusion).
facts.source_location: see P2 claim; USHMM on persecution

facts.text: UGLE has around 175,000 members in England and Wales; worldwide estimates range from about 2 to over 6 million.
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Freemasonry (WebFetch notes research/britannica_freemasonry_webfetch.txt); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freemasonry (secondary; research/wiki_freemasonry.txt) ('two million to more than six million')

facts.text: Lodge meetings: administrative business (minutes, balloting new members, charity news), then ceremonies, then dining together.

facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Freemasonry (WebFetch notes research/britannica_freemasonry_webfetch.txt) (Supreme Being; women's lodges in Britain)

facts.text: Templar seal: two knights on one horse, emphasising poverty.
facts.source_location: 'Their emblem was of two knights riding on a single horse, emphasizing the order's poverty'

facts.text: William of Tyre: after nine years there were still only nine.
facts.source: William of Tyre, Historia XII.7 (c.1170–84), trans. E.A. Babcock & A.C. Krey, via Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/tyre-templars.asp (local research/fordham_tyre.txt)
facts.source_location: 'after nine years ... there were still only nine of them'

facts.text: Council of Troyes, January 1129 (1128 old style) gave the order a rule.
facts.corroboration: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Templars (Britannica; WebFetch notes research/britannica_templars_webfetch_2026-10-25.txt) ('Council of Troyes in 1128')

facts.text: Bernard of Clairvaux backed the order; wrote In Praise of the New Knighthood (c.1136).
facts.source_location: 'may have requested that Bernard of Clairvaux compose the new rule. Bernard also wrote In Praise of the New Knighthood (c. 1136)'

facts.text: Rule modelled on Benedictine/Cistercian life: poverty, chastity, obedience; dormitory; communal meals; no gambling/drunkenness; primary duty to fight.
facts.source_location: 'modeled after the Benedictine Rule ... oath of poverty, chastity, and obedience ... not allowed to gamble, swear, or become drunk ... common dormitory and eating meals together ... primary duty was to fight'

facts.text: Knights wore white with red cross (cross added later, under Eugene III); sergeants (majority) in black; most could not read Latin.
facts.source_location: 'white surcoat marked with a red cross ... sergeants ... majority ... black habits'; 'unable to read Latin'
facts.corroboration: William of Tyre, Historia XII.7 (c.1170–84), trans. E.A. Babcock & A.C. Krey, via Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/tyre-templars.asp (local research/fordham_tyre.txt) (red cross under Pope Eugenius)

facts.text: 1139 bull (Innocent II, Omne datum optimum): exempt from tithes and from bishops; subject to pope alone.
facts.source_location: 'not required to pay the tithe ... exempt from episcopal jurisdiction, being subject to the pope alone'

facts.text: Castles, garrisons, battles; after Hattin (1187) Saladin executed captured Templars.
facts.source_location: 'bought the Templars who were taken prisoner and later had each of them executed'

facts.text: Donations of property across Europe; houses (preceptories) sent revenue east.
facts.source_location: significant donations; 'each individual house, called a preceptory'
facts.corroboration: Inner Temple Yearbook, 'The Knights Templar: the first bankers?' https://www.innertemple.org.uk (local research/inner_temple_bankers.txt)

facts.text: Moved bullion safely; attractive as bankers to kings and pilgrims.

facts.text: Medici: Florentine banking family; largest banking network in Europe; Cosimo's patronage shaped Florence (ep04).
facts.source_location: 'The family's banking network, the largest in Europe'; Giovanni di Bicci (1360–1429) banking

facts.text: Sunday Mass in Florence Cathedral, 26 April 1478; Lorenzo and Giuliano present.
The Medici began as bankers and produced dukes, popes and queens.
The Medici were driven out of Florence more than once (1433, 1494, 1527).
Anna Maria Luisa ensured the collections stayed in Florence (Family Pact).

facts.text: Florence a merchant republic rich from wool, cloth and banking; the florin trusted across Europe.
The Medici came from the Mugello and were not old nobility.
Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici (c.1360–1429) made the family great.
1397: Giovanni moved his bank from Rome to Florence; the Medici Bank dates from that year.
facts.corroboration: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (Harvard UP, 1963)

facts.text: Branches in Rome, Venice, then Geneva, later Bruges, London, Avignon, Milan.
facts.corroboration: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (Harvard UP, 1963)

facts.text: Bills of exchange allowed payment in one city and repayment in another without moving coin.
facts.corroboration: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (Harvard UP, 1963)

facts.text: The Church condemned interest as usury; exchange profits arguably avoided it.
facts.corroboration: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (Harvard UP, 1963)

facts.text: The Medici became bankers to the papal court.
1427: Rome branch held c.100,000 florins of curial deposits; Rome for a time earned more than half the profits.
facts.corroboration: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (Harvard UP, 1963)

facts.text: Giovanni died 1429, buried in the (Old) Sacristy at San Lorenzo.
Cosimo represented the bank at the Council of Constance and managed papal finances.
Cosimo very probably the richest man in Europe.
facts.source_location: research/britannica_and_institutions_webfetch_2026-10-26.md §BrC ('certainly the wealthiest man of his time')

facts.text: Rinaldo degli Albizzi's faction; Cosimo summoned and locked in the Palazzo Vecchio, September 1433.
Feared poison; jailer tasted food; bribery; sentence became exile.
facts.uncertainty: Anecdote from the chronicle tradition; detail cannot be verified

facts.text: Exile to Padua then Venice; received with honour.
1434: new government recalled Cosimo; his enemies exiled.
Cosimo rarely held office; 30 years of dominance.
Kept republican forms; manipulated lot-drawing (scrutinies).
Brunelleschi closing the dome in 1434; paid for by the city and the Wool Guild (Arte della Lana); consecrated 25 March 1436.
facts.source_location: Cornerstone History ep04 claims (Opera del Duomo, Arte della Lana)

facts.text: Cosimo backed rebuilding of San Lorenzo; Brunelleschi designed the Old Sacristy.
Cosimo is said to have rejected Brunelleschi's palace design as too grand; chose Michelozzo.
Michelozzo rebuilt San Marco; Fra Angelico frescoed the cells; Cosimo endowed a public library.
Donatello's bronze David: first freestanding nude since antiquity; made for the Medici; in their palace courtyard.
1439 Council of Florence; Cosimo helped bring it; Greek and Latin churches sought union.
Union failed; Platonic revival; Ficino given a house near Careggi to translate Plato.
Cosimo died 1464; titled Pater Patriae 1465.
Piero the Gouty ruled 1464–69; 1469 Lorenzo (20) and Giuliano succeeded.
The Pazzi had taken over papal banking from the Medici.
Sixtus IV knew of the plot; Riario, Salviati and the Pazzi conspired.
26 April 1478: Giuliano killed, Lorenzo wounded, refuge in sacristy; Salviati failed at Palazzo Vecchio and was hanged from a window; people backed the Medici.
Bandini fled to Constantinople, extradited, hanged 1479; Leonardo sketched him.
War with the Pope and Naples; Lorenzo went to Naples himself (1479–80).
Ficino, Poliziano, Pico; Botticelli, Verrocchio, Leonardo in the Medici world.
Sculpture garden near San Marco; Michelangelo c.1490 taken into the palace like a son.
Branches in London, Bruges, Lyon failed: poor management and bad loans to princes.
facts.corroboration: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (Harvard UP, 1963)

facts.text: Lorenzo died at Careggi April 1492, aged 43.
Story of Savonarola refusing absolution is a legend disproved by documents (Ridolfi).
1494 Charles VIII invaded; Piero yielded fortresses; Medici expelled Nov 1494; palace looted.
Medici Bank collapsed with the family's fall, 1494.
facts.corroboration: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (Harvard UP, 1963)

facts.text: 7 Feb 1497 bonfire of the vanities; Botticelli story not supported by early sources; loss of art slight.
Alexander VI excommunicated Savonarola 1497; hanged and burned 23 May 1498 in Piazza della Signoria.
Giovanni made cardinal at 13; Medici restored 1512; elected Leo X 1513.
Leo's spending; St Peter's; indulgences; Luther excommunicated 1521.
Clement VII (Giulio, son of Giuliano) pope 1523; Sack of Rome May 1527; Medici expelled 1527; siege until 1530; Alessandro duke 1532; refused Henry VIII annulment; Last Judgement 1534.
Alessandro murdered 1537 by Lorenzino; Cosimo I (17) succeeds; conquers Siena; Grand Duke 1569.
Uffizi built as offices by Vasari; Francesco made the upper floor a gallery.
Francesco and Bianca died 1587 within a day; poison rumours; 2006 arsenic study vs 2010 malaria finding.
facts.corroboration: Fornaciari et al., Am J Med 2010;123(6):568–9

facts.text: Galileo named Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars (1610) for Cosimo II and brothers.
Catherine b. 1519, orphaned within weeks; married 1533 to Henry (king 1547); three sons kings; St Bartholomew's 1572; blame debated.
Poisoner legends (Jeanne d'Albret's gloves) come from hostile writers; no evidence.
Marie de' Medici Queen of France; Medici blood in the French royal line.
Donatello, the leading sculptor of the age, was close to Cosimo.
Lorenzo known as 'il Magnifico'.
facts.uncertainty: Honorific also used of other notables

facts.text: Lorenzo's diplomacy helped keep a balance among the Italian states.
Savonarola preached at San Marco from 1490: Church corrupt, Italy to be scourged, Florence to repent.
After 1494 Savonarola backed a broader republic (Great Council) and preached against vice.
Gian Gastone childless; powers agreed Tuscany to Francis Stephen of Lorraine (1735–37).
Gian Gastone d. 9 July 1737; Anna Maria Luisa; Family Pact signed Vienna 31 Oct 1737; Art. III conditions.
facts.source: https://www.toscana.beniculturali.it (Segretariato regionale MiC Toscana: Anna Maria Luisa de' Medici e il Patto di Famiglia)

facts.text: She died 1743 and was buried at San Lorenzo.
facts.source: https://www.toscana.beniculturali.it (Segretariato regionale MiC Toscana: Anna Maria Luisa de' Medici e il Patto di Famiglia)

facts.text: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79; date debated (Aug vs Oct)
Pompeii and Herculaneum were buried under metres of ash and pumice and lay hidden until the 18th c.
Oscans founded first settlements (8th c. BC); Greek and Samnite influence; site near mouth of the Sarno
Population c. 11000-11500 by household counts; fertile land
Sulla besieged Pompeii 89 BC; ballista impact marks in walls; became Colonia Cornelia Veneria Pompeianorum with veterans settled
Forum temples theatres baths; amphitheatre among earliest surviving stone amphitheatres (c. 70 BC)
Paved streets with raised pavements and stepping stones; bakeries workshops
Thermopolia (street bars) with dolia counters
Electoral notices painted on walls and many thousands of graffiti
House of the Faun and the Alexander Mosaic
AD 59 amphitheatre riot Pompeians vs Nucerians; Senate banned games ten years; fresco records it
Severe earthquake 5 Feb 62 (Seneca NQ 6.1; some date to 63); damage to Pompeii Herculaneum Nuceria
Repairs from the quake still under way in 79; Temple of Isis rebuilt in name of six-year-old N. Popidius Celsinus (inscription)
Vesuvius had not erupted in living memory; Pliny the Younger's two letters to Tacitus are the only surviving eyewitness account
Pliny's mother pointed out the cloud about 1 pm; he likened it to a pine tree (quoted from Melmoth translation)
Tremors for days before not alarming as frequent in Campania
Plinian column 27-33 km; wind blew SE over Pompeii; pumice fall collapsed roofs; term Plinian
About 1150 bodies found at Pompeii; many escapees carried valuables; many fled

Rectina's appeal; warships launched; 'Fortune favours the brave'; landed at Stabiae with Pomponianus

Younger Pliny's flight at Misenum: black cloud; darkness like a shut room; shrieks screams shouts; ash like snow (Melmoth wording)
Herculaneum smaller wealthier (c. 5000); buried c. 20 m; organic material carbonised
Belief most escaped; 1980s excavation of shoreline boathouses found c. 300 skeletons
Villa of the Papyri probably of L. Calpurnius Piso (Caesar's father-in-law); only ancient library surviving largely intact; scrolls being read
Towns not rebuilt; locations forgotten; hill called La Civita

1592 Domenico Fontana's underground channel cut through Pompeii hitting painted walls
Herculaneum: 1709 well (d'Elbeuf); 1738 excavations under Charles of Bourbon by tunnelling

Early digging was treasure-hunting; frescoes cut out; Grand Tour; influence on European taste

Garden of the Fugitives: 13 victims

Göbekli Tepe, SE Turkey; inhabited c. 9500 BC to at least 8000 BC (Pre-Pottery Neolithic); T-shaped pillars; >5,000 years before Giza (c. 2560 BC)
Klaus Schmidt recognised significance 1994, excavated from 1995
Pillars up to ~5.5 m in enclosures; carved animals (foxes, boars, snakes, vultures); monolithic limestone pillars weighing tons; Neolithic stone tools
Pre-Pottery Neolithic: before pottery; writing and wheel much later; builders at transition to farming; monumental building before cities
Popularly 'world's first temple' (Schmidt); domestic buildings and rainwater cisterns forced revision of temple narrative
UNESCO World Heritage 2018: 'one of the first manifestations of human-made monumental architecture'; changed views of Neolithic
Knossos, Crete: often called Europe's oldest city; inhabited from Neolithic; largest centre of Minoan civilisation (Bronze Age)
Arthur Evans excavated from 1900: palace, courts, staircases, light wells, drainage, wall paintings; named 'Minoan' after myth of Minos
Evans reconstructed parts in reinforced concrete; Minoan decline c. 1450 BC; rediscovered by excavation in early 20th c.
Myths of Minos, labyrinth, Minotaur associated with Knossos
Linear B tablets at Knossos; deciphered 1952 by Michael Ventris building on Alice Kober; earliest written Greek; Linear A undeciphered
Carthage, Tunisia; traditional founding 814 BC by Phoenicians from Tyre; Dido founding story legendary
Carthage became major Mediterranean trading/naval power
Punic Wars 264–146 BC; Hannibal left Spain 218 BC with army and elephants, crossed Alps; 15-year occupation of much of Italy; Rome near defeat then recovered
146 BC destroyed after nearly three-year siege; final assault six days; on last day 50,000 prisoners taken, sold into slavery
Claim Carthage was sown with salt dates from at least 1863; no evidence
End of Punic Wars ended Carthaginian power, Rome dominant in western Mediterranean
Persepolis, Fars, Iran: ceremonial capital of Achaemenid Empire; terrace and palaces built by Darius I (from c. 518 BC)
Achaemenid Empire largest empire of its time; from Egypt/Balkans to Indus
Satrapies under satraps; Royal Road Susa–Sardis 2,699 km; mounted couriers nine days; model influenced later empires
Apadana stairway reliefs show delegations of subject peoples bringing tribute
Taken by Alexander 330 BC; wooden parts soon destroyed by fire; accident or revenge for burning of Athens' Acropolis unclear
Giza, outskirts of Cairo; Great Pyramid built for Khufu c. 2560 BC
146.6 m; tallest human-made structure >3,700 years; ~2.3 million blocks; oldest of Seven Wonders, only one largely intact
Greeks believed slave labour; workers' camps suggest thousands of conscript labourers; workers' village at Giza; state organisation
Great Wall: Qin linked earlier walls; successive dynasties expanded; best-known sections Ming (1368–1644); rammed earth; system of walls, towers, forts
Qin Shi Huang unified China 221 BC, first emperor; standardised script, weights and measures, currency
2012 survey: all sections total 21,196 km
Visible-from-space claim questionable; Yang Liwei said he could not see it
Constantinople capital of Roman/Byzantine Empire from 330 to 1453; sole capital after western loss in 5th c.; Theodosian walls (5th c.) held off besiegers for most of a millennium
Hagia Sophia completed 537 by Justinian I; world's largest interior space; largest church >500 years; museum 1935, mosque 2020
Justinian's codification of Roman law (Corpus Juris Civilis, from 528); basis of later civil law
Fell to Ottomans under Mehmed II 29 May 1453 after 53-day siege; Hagia Sophia made a mosque; Ottoman capital; often used to mark end of Middle Ages
Jerusalem one of oldest cities; holy to Judaism, Christianity, Islam
Hebrew Bible: First Temple built by Solomon, 10th c. BC; destroyed by Babylonians 587/586 BC
Return from exile after Persian conquest of Babylon, Second Temple built; destroyed AD 70 by Romans under Titus
Christian tradition: crucifixion/resurrection of Jesus in Jerusalem; third holiest city in Islam

Christians ~31.1% and Muslims ~24.1% of world population (plus Jews): more than half (editorial inference on 'matters most')
Uruk, southern Iraq; c. 2900 BC (Uruk period end) ~300 ha and perhaps 40,000 inhabitants; among first cities
Eanna district: writing and monumental public architecture emerged (Uruk VI–IV, c. 3300 BC); proto-cuneiform tablets c. 3300 BC
Kushim tablets (c. 3400–3000 BC) record barley; oldest known written personal name (if an individual), perhaps an accountant

Cuneiform: earliest known writing system; used c. 31st c. BC–2nd c. AD for many languages; rediscovered via Persepolis inscriptions, deciphered 19th c.; writing as foundation of records (interpretive)
Acropolis of Athens; Parthenon

Women, slaves, metics excluded
Parthenon begun 447 BC, substantially complete 432; Delian League funds/treasury; 1687 Venetian shell hit Ottoman powder store
5th-century Athens: history (Herodotus, Thucydides), drama, philosophy (Socrates); neoclassical columns legacy (interpretive)
Epic of Gilgamesh: Gilgamesh builds Uruk's walls; Sumerian King List places him 27th c. BC; historicity uncertain
The Vatican area (Ager Vaticanus) lay across the Tiber outside the ancient city; marshy ground with the Vatican Hill behind.
Vatican City grew from the site of St Peter's tomb and basilica and the papal palace to a sovereign state in 1929.
A circus (racetrack) on the Vatican was begun by Caligula and completed/associated with Nero (Circus of Gaius and Nero).
Roman cemeteries/necropolis lined the roads on the Vatican slope.
Great Fire of Rome AD 64; Nero blamed and persecuted Christians (Tacitus).
Tradition holds Peter was martyred near the Vatican circus and buried nearby; inverted crucifixion is from later (apocryphal Acts of Peter) tradition; no contemporary burial record.
facts.uncertainty: Historicity of Roman death debated (consensus favours Roman martyrdom)

facts.text: A small aedicula (Trophy of Gaius) c.160 stood over a grave; the presbyter Gaius (c.200, quoted by Eusebius) said he could show the 'trophies' of the apostles on the Vatican.
facts.uncertainty: Identification with Peter's grave is tradition

facts.text: Constantine ordered Old St Peter's built (begun c.318-322) with the altar over the monument believed to be Peter's grave.
Builders cut into the hill and filled the necropolis to create a platform; the basilica had five aisles, an atrium, and was over 100 m long.
Old St Peter's stood for some 12 centuries as a major pilgrimage church.
Charlemagne was crowned emperor in Old St Peter's on Christmas Day 800.
Until Avignon the popes' main residence and cathedral were at the Lateran.
The Vatican lay outside the Aurelian Walls.
Stephen II appealed to Pippin against the Lombards; Pippin's 756 donation of conquered lands founded the Papal States.
The Papal States: central Italian territory under papal sovereignty 756-1870; pope as temporal ruler.
After the 846 Arab raid on St Peter's, Leo IV built the Leonine Wall 848-852 enclosing the Vatican Hill; parts survive.
Avignon Papacy 1309-1376/77; Clement V (Gascon, archbishop of Bordeaux) settled in Avignon in 1309.
Gregory XI returned 1377; Lateran Palace badly damaged by fires of 1307 and 1361; the Vatican became the principal papal residence.
The Passetto di Borgo, a fortified corridor (built 1277 by Nicholas III) links the Vatican to Castel Sant'Angelo (Hadrian's mausoleum).
By the 15th century Old St Peter's was falling into disrepair; earlier popes (Nicholas V) planned rebuilding.
Julius II chose Bramante's design; foundation stone laid 18 April 1506.
Bramante's plan was centralised with a great dome; much of the old basilica was demolished.
facts.uncertainty: Demolition was gradual over a century

facts.text: The Swiss Guard entered Rome 22 January 1506 under Julius II, the official founding date.
Julius II (d.1513) and Bramante (d.1514) died early; successive architects changed plans; a protective structure (tegurio) covered the high altar during works.
Sack of Rome began 6 May 1527 by mutinous troops of Charles V; looting continued for months.
147 of 189 Swiss Guards incl. commander Kaspar Röist died; Clement VII escaped via the Passetto to Castel Sant'Angelo.
New Swiss Guard recruits are sworn in each 6 May.
Michelangelo took over St Peter's c.1546-47 aged ~71, returned to a central plan, worked unpaid (as commonly reported) until death in 1564.
facts.uncertainty: Unpaid status is from contemporary accounts (Vasari)

facts.text: Dome completed 1590 by Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana; ~136 m tall; Maderno extended nave and façade (1607-1614); consecrated 18 Nov 1626.
France withdrew from Rome in 1870 (Franco-Prussian War, Sedan 1 Sept); Italian artillery breached the Aurelian Walls near Porta Pia on 20 Sept 1870.
Pius IX wanted only token resistance to show the city was taken by force; Kanzler capitulated the same day.
Plebiscite 2 Oct 1870 annexed Rome; Rome became capital in 1871.
Law of Guarantees 1871 rejected by Pius IX; popes stayed in the Vatican as 'prisoners' until 1929; first blessings from inside St Peter's (Leo XIII to Benedict XV).
facts.uncertainty: Pius XI gave the blessing from the outer loggia in 1922

facts.text: Bernini's bronze baldacchino over the papal altar (1623-34).
Bernini's colonnade (1656-1667) described in his own expression as 'the maternal arms of Mother Church'.
The Vatican obelisk, from the circus, was moved to the square in 1586 by Domenico Fontana.
By the 17th c. the basilica and square took their present form.
Napoleonic France occupied the Papal States (1798, 1809); Pius VI and Pius VII were taken to France; Congress of Vienna restored most territory.
1859-60 most Papal States annexed; 27 Mar 1861 parliament proclaimed Rome capital; French garrison protected Rome.
Vatican City covers 0.44 km2 (44 ha), the smallest independent state.
Vatican City has its own flag.
Pius XI (elected Feb 1922) and Mussolini (PM Oct 1922); secret negotiations from 1926; Lateran Pacts signed 11 Feb 1929 at the Lateran Palace by Gasparri and Mussolini.

Pacts: Treaty, Concordat, Financial Convention; Italy recognised Holy See sovereignty over Vatican City; Holy See recognised Kingdom of Italy with Rome capital; preamble: 'absolute and visible independence'.
Financial Convention: 750 million lire cash + 1 billion lire in 5% bonds.
Poste Vaticane created 1929; stamps from 1 Aug 1929.
Vatican Radio built by Marconi; first broadcast 12 Feb 1931.
Vatican railway: Lateran Treaty Art. 6; ~300 m of track, station built 1929-33; first used by a pope (John XXIII) 1962; shortest national railway.
IOR (Vatican Bank) founded 27 June 1942 by Pius XII.
Via della Conciliazione built 1936-1950 by demolishing the Spina di Borgo.
Swiss Guard ~135 members (2024); unmarried Swiss Catholic men 19-30; Renaissance-style uniform.
Resident population a few hundred (est. ~500-800 depending on source); citizenship tied to office/employment, lost when it ends (Law on Citizenship 2011).
Absolute monarchy; Pope holds full legislative, executive and judicial power.
Boundary is walls except across St Peter's Square, marked by a travertine strip between the colonnade ends.
1939 work in the grottoes (for Pius XI's tomb) led to Pius XII's excavations of the necropolis (1940-49), which found the aedicula.
Identification of bones as Peter's (Paul VI 1968) is disputed among scholars.
Nicholas V (1447-55) planned rebuilding the Vatican quarter and founded the Vatican Library collection; palace expanded by successors.
Holy See vs Vatican City distinct; Holy See conducts diplomacy, UN permanent observer since 1964; relations with 184 states (Jan 2026).
